The reference is unchanged in content, but every concept card now ends with a challenge adapted from the
local TMUA Paper 2 archive and the MAT, STEP-foundation and ECAA papers. The problems are harder than the
originals they come from: each is multi-part, and several ask you to decide a claim *and* supply the
counterexample. Attempt a problem before opening its solution.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Where the marks are, from eight years of papers.** Necessary/sufficient **25 %** · straight calculation
**28 %** · quantifiers **15 %** · spot the error **10 %** · converse/contrapositive **8 %** ·
counterexample **7 %**. Divisors and primes carry about **13 %** of the questions, and a plane shape asked
as a logical condition appears in **every** sitting.
:::

### S1 · Statement forms ★

$$A\Rightarrow B\;=\;\text{“if }A\text{ then }B\text{”}\;=\;\text{“}A\text{ only if }B\text{”}\;=\;\text{“}B\text{ if }A\text{”}$$

**The bare "if" introduces the forcing statement.** So "$A$ **if** $B$" is $B\Rightarrow A$ — backwards from
the reading order.

"$A$ **if and only if** $B$" is both arrows: $A\Leftrightarrow B$.

**Reversed wording:** in "a condition **for** $Q$ is $P$", the target follows the word *for*. Find the
target first, then the condition.

[the trap: "only if" points forwards, "if" points backwards]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
Let $n$ be a positive integer and put

$$P:\ n\text{ is divisible by }6,\qquad Q:\ n\text{ is even},\qquad R:\ n\text{ is divisible by }3 .$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Rewrite each sentence as an implication between the labels, then say whether it is true.
Exactly one of them is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;(i) $P$ only if $Q$. &nbsp;&nbsp; (ii) $Q$ if $P$. &nbsp;&nbsp;
(iii) A condition for $Q$ is $P$. &nbsp;&nbsp; (iv) $Q$ is necessary for $P$. &nbsp;&nbsp;
(v) $P$ unless $Q$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Write $P$ as an "if and only if" statement built from $Q$ and $R$, and justify it.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** A multiple-choice question offers these two options about $P$:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** &nbsp;$P$ is true **if** $n$ is divisible by $12$. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
**B** &nbsp;$P$ is true **if and only if** $n$ is divisible by $12$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;Exactly one is correct. Which, and what refutes the other?

[Adapted from **2022 P2 Q5** (a statement, its converse and its contrapositive) and **2019 P2 Q17** ("true if" against "true if and only if").]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)**

| | sentence | implication | true? |
|---|---|---|---|
| (i) | $P$ only if $Q$ | $P\Rightarrow Q$ | **yes** |
| (ii) | $Q$ if $P$ | $P\Rightarrow Q$ | **yes** |
| (iii) | a condition for $Q$ is $P$ | $P\Rightarrow Q$ | **yes** |
| (iv) | $Q$ is necessary for $P$ | $P\Rightarrow Q$ | **yes** |
| (v) | $P$ unless $Q$ | $\lnot Q\Rightarrow P$ | **no** |

*The first four are the same implication in four disguises.* "Only if" points forwards; the bare "if" points
backwards, so (ii) reverses to $P\Rightarrow Q$ as well; in (iii) the target follows the word *for*, so $Q$
is the target; and "necessary" points backwards from $Q$ to $P$ — which is again $P\Rightarrow Q$. Every one
of them is true, because $6\mid n$ forces $2\mid n$.

**(v)** is the odd one out. "$P$ unless $Q$" means *$P$ holds in the absence of $Q$*, i.e.
$\lnot Q\Rightarrow P$: every **odd** $n$ would have to be divisible by $6$.

$$\boxed{n=5\text{ refutes (v)}}$$

**(b)** $\boxed{P\iff(Q\text{ and }R)}$, that is $6\mid n\iff\left(2\mid n\text{ and }3\mid n\right)$.

*Both directions are needed.* Forwards is immediate. Backwards: $2$ and $3$ share no factor, so if both
divide $n$ then so does their product. *(With $4$ and $6$ in place of $2$ and $3$ this fails — $n=12$ is
divisible by both but not by $24$.)*

**(c)** $\boxed{\textbf{A}}$. "$P$ is true if $12\mid n$" is $12\mid n\Rightarrow6\mid n$, which holds.

**B** claims the converse as well, $6\mid n\Rightarrow12\mid n$, and $n=6$ refutes it.

*This is the standard pair of distractors: an "if" option and an "if and only if" option differing by one
arrow. Test the extra arrow and one of them dies.*
:::

### S2 · Converse and contrapositive ★

| | form | equivalent to the original? |
|---|---|---|
| statement | $A\Rightarrow B$ | — |
| **converse** | $B\Rightarrow A$ | **no** |
| inverse | $\lnot A\Rightarrow\lnot B$ | **no** |
| **contrapositive** | $\lnot B\Rightarrow\lnot A$ | **always yes** |

The inverse and the converse are contrapositives *of each other*, so they stand or fall together.

When a question asks **"which must be true"**, the answer is almost always the contrapositive and the
**converse is the trap option**.

**The standard question: "which is logically equivalent?"** You are being asked to find one of

$$\text{if }P\text{ then }Q
\ \ \equiv\ \ P\ \textbf{only if}\ Q
\ \ \equiv\ \ \lnot Q\Rightarrow\lnot P .$$

**Method: symbolise the whole sentence first, then swap and negate.** Write $P$ and $Q$ down as labels,
read the sentence into $P\Rightarrow Q$, then exchange the two sides **and** negate both. Never try to
rearrange the English directly.

[negate a compound with De Morgan — see S4]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
A straight line $L$ passes through $(1,2)$ and is neither horizontal nor vertical. Let $P$ be the statement

> if the $y$-intercept of $L$ is negative, then the $x$-intercept of $L$ is positive.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Write down the converse and the contrapositive of $P$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Taking the gradient as $m$, express both intercepts in terms of $m$, and hence **prove**
that $P$ is true.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Decide whether the converse is true. If it is not, give the equation of a line through
$(1,2)$ that refutes it.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** Explain why parts (b) and (c) together settle the contrapositive with no further work.

[Adapted from **2022 P2 Q5**, where the same line and statement appear; here the intercepts must actually be computed and the converse refuted.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** With $Y$: "the $y$-intercept is negative" and $X$: "the $x$-intercept is positive", $P$ is
$Y\Rightarrow X$, so

$$\text{converse: } X\Rightarrow Y,\qquad \text{contrapositive: } \lnot X\Rightarrow\lnot Y .$$

In words: the converse is "if the $x$-intercept is positive then the $y$-intercept is negative"; the
contrapositive is "if the $x$-intercept is not positive then the $y$-intercept is not negative".

**(b)** The line is $y=m(x-1)+2$ with $m\ne0$, so

$$y\text{-intercept}=2-m,\qquad x\text{-intercept}=1-\frac{2}{m}.$$

*Now translate the hypothesis into a condition on $m$:* $2-m<0$ means $m>2$. For such $m$ we have
$0<\dfrac{2}{m}<1$, hence

$$1-\frac{2}{m}>0 .$$

So the $x$-intercept is positive and $\boxed{P\text{ is true}}$.

**(c)** The converse is **false**. *Solve the hypothesis instead of the conclusion:*
$1-\dfrac{2}{m}>0$ holds when $m>2$ **or** $m<0$ — and the second branch is not covered by $m>2$.

Take $m=-1$, giving $y=-(x-1)+2$:

$$\boxed{x+y=3}$$

Its $x$-intercept is $3>0$, but its $y$-intercept is $3$, which is not negative.

**(d)** A statement and its contrapositive are logically equivalent — they are true or false together — so
(b) makes the contrapositive **true**. No separate argument is possible or needed. *The converse is the
trap option precisely because it is the one rearrangement that is **not** equivalent.*
:::

### S3 · Necessary and sufficient ★

$$\text{“}P\text{ sufficient for }Q\text{”}=P\Rightarrow Q\qquad
\text{“}P\text{ necessary for }Q\text{”}=Q\Rightarrow P$$

**Sufficient points forwards; necessary points backwards.**

**The routine that answers every one of these.** Write the *exact* set of cases making each statement
true, then compare by inclusion:

$$P\subset Q\Rightarrow\textbf{sufficient, not necessary}\qquad
Q\subset P\Rightarrow\textbf{necessary, not sufficient}$$
$$P=Q\Rightarrow\textbf{both}\qquad\text{overlapping}\Rightarrow\textbf{neither}$$

**The tip: turn every "necessary" into a "sufficient".** The two words describe the same arrow from opposite
ends, so

"$X$ is **necessary** for $Y$" &nbsp;=&nbsp; "$Y$ is **sufficient** for $X$".

Rewrite the question that way and you only ever have to think in **one** direction.

**Then: the sufficient one is always the more restricted condition — the smaller set.** Of the two, whichever
is **harder to satisfy** is sufficient for the other; the easier one is necessary.

[25 % of recent papers — the largest single block of marks]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
Let $a$, $b$ and $n$ be positive integers and let

$$(*):\ ab\text{ is divisible by }n .$$

Classify each condition below as **sufficient but not necessary**, **necessary but not sufficient**,
**both**, or **neither** for $(*)$ — and support every "not" with an explicit counterexample.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** $n$ divides $a$, or $n$ divides $b$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** $n$ divides $ab^{2}$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** $n$ divides $a+b$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** $\dfrac{n}{\gcd(n,a)}$ divides $b$.

[Adapted from **2019 P2 Q5**, which asks only about condition (a); **2021 P2 Q4** is the same divisibility trap stated as a counterexample question.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

*Use the S3 routine: ask one direction at a time, and hunt for a counterexample the moment a direction looks
doubtful.*

**(a) Sufficient but not necessary.** If $n\mid a$ then $n\mid ab$, and likewise for $b$ — so the condition
forces $(*)$.

It is not necessary: $\boxed{a=2,\ b=2,\ n=4}$ gives $ab=4$, divisible by $4$, yet $4$ divides neither $a$
nor $b$. *The factors of $n$ can be split between $a$ and $b$ instead of sitting inside one of them.*

**(b) Necessary but not sufficient.** If $n\mid ab$ then $n\mid ab\cdot b=ab^{2}$, so the condition must
hold.

It is not sufficient: $\boxed{a=1,\ b=2,\ n=4}$ gives $ab^{2}=4$, divisible by $4$, but $ab=2$ is not.

**(c) Neither.** Not sufficient: $a=b=1$, $n=2$ gives $a+b=2$ divisible by $2$, while $ab=1$ is not. Not
necessary: $a=1$, $b=2$, $n=2$ gives $ab=2$ divisible by $2$, while $a+b=3$ is not.

$$\boxed{\text{neither direction holds}}$$

**(d) Both — this is the exact condition.** Write $g=\gcd(n,a)$. Then $n\mid ab$ holds precisely when
$\dfrac{n}{g}\ \Big|\ \dfrac{a}{g}\,b$, and $\dfrac{n}{g}$ and $\dfrac{a}{g}$ share no factor, so by
Euclid's lemma this happens exactly when $\dfrac{n}{g}\mid b$.

$$\boxed{\text{necessary and sufficient}}$$

*Note how (a) and (d) are related: (a) is the special case $g=n$ or $g=1$. The exam's favourite distractor is
to offer the special case and call it the condition.*
:::

### S4 · Quantifiers and negation ★

$$\lnot(\forall x,\;P)=\exists x,\;\lnot P\qquad\lnot(\exists x,\;P)=\forall x,\;\lnot P$$

The negation of "**all** X are Y" is "**some** X is **not** Y" — *not* "no X is Y".

**De Morgan.** $\lnot(P\text{ and }Q)=\lnot P\text{ or }\lnot Q$; $\lnot(P\text{ or }Q)=\lnot P\text{ and }\lnot Q$.

**Negating an implication.** $\lnot(P\Rightarrow Q)=P\;\textbf{and}\;\lnot Q$ — never "if $P$ then not $Q$".

**Order matters.** $\forall x\,\exists y$ lets $y$ depend on $x$; $\exists y\,\forall x$ needs one $y$ for
all $x$ at once — far stronger.

[to negate a chain, flip every quantifier in order, then the inside]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Decide whether each statement is true, with a reason or a counterexample.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I. $\ \forall x\in\mathbb R\ \ \forall n\in\mathbb Z^{+}:\ x<n$
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;II. $\ \forall x\in\mathbb R\ \ \exists n\in\mathbb Z^{+}:\ x<n$
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;III. $\ \exists x\in\mathbb R\ \ \forall n\in\mathbb Z^{+}:\ x<n$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Negate each of I, II and III, and check your answers to (a) against them.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** For how many real $x$ is the following true?

$$(\ast)\ \ \exists y\in\mathbb R:\ x-xy+y<0$$

[Adapted from **2022 P2 Q10** (the three quantifier orders) and **2022 P2 Q13** (the $\exists y$ count), combined into one question.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)**

**I is false.** *One pair kills a $\forall\forall$:* take $x=5$ and $n=1$.

**II is true.** Given $x$, choose $n=\lfloor x\rfloor+1$ if $x\ge0$ and $n=1$ otherwise; either way $n>x$.
*Here $n$ is allowed to depend on $x$, which is the whole difference from I.*

**III is true.** *A single $x$ must work for every $n$ at once* — and $x=0$ does, since every positive
integer is at least $1>0$. (Any negative $x$ works too.)

**(b)** Flip each quantifier in order, then negate the inside; $\lnot(x<n)$ is $x\ge n$.

| | negation | truth |
|---|---|---|
| I | $\exists x\ \exists n:\ x\ge n$ | **true** |
| II | $\exists x\ \forall n:\ x\ge n$ | **false** |
| III | $\forall x\ \exists n:\ x\ge n$ | **false** |

*Each negation has the opposite truth value to the original, which is the check.* Note that II and the
negation of III say almost the same thing with the inequality reversed — II is the Archimedean property,
and its failure would mean some real number exceeds every positive integer.

**(c)** *Collect the $y$ terms, because $y$ is the variable we are allowed to choose:*

$$x-xy+y=x+y(1-x).$$

**If $x\ne1$** the coefficient $1-x$ is non-zero, so $y(1-x)$ can be made as large and negative as we like;
some $y$ certainly drives the total below $0$. So $(\ast)$ holds.

**If $x=1$** the expression collapses to $1-y+y=1$ for *every* $y$, and $1<0$ is false. So $(\ast)$ fails.

$$\boxed{(\ast)\text{ is true for all real }x\text{ except }x=1}$$

*The question is really "for which $x$ does the $y$ actually disappear?" — a $\forall\exists$ problem solved
by looking at the coefficient, not by trying values.*
:::

### S5 · Proof methods

- **Direct** — assume the hypothesis, deduce the conclusion. Represent generally ($2k$, $2k+1$).
- **By cases** — split by remainder; check every case.
- **By contradiction** — assume the negation, derive an absurdity.
- **By counterexample** — to disprove "for all", one case is enough.

**A counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis *and* fail the conclusion.** A case where the hypothesis
fails proves nothing.

**"Possible" is $\exists$** — produce one witness. **"Must" is $\forall$** — one counterexample destroys it.

[read which one you were given before starting]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
Consider this claim about positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$:

> if $a$ divides $bc$, then $a$ divides $b$ or $a$ divides $c$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Which of the following are counterexamples?

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I. $a=5,\ b=10,\ c=20$ &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
II. $a=8,\ b=4,\ c=4$ &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
III. $a=6,\ b=7,\ c=12$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** State the extra hypothesis on $a$ that turns the claim into a theorem, and name the
theorem.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Prove or disprove: if $a$ divides $bc$ and $\gcd(a,b)=1$, then $a$ divides $c$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** The claim "$\lvert a+b\rvert<\lvert a\rvert+\lvert b\rvert$ for all real $a,b$" is
false. State the correct version, and describe **every** case in which your version is an equality.

[Adapted from **2021 P2 Q4** (the three candidate counterexamples, verbatim) and **2020 P2 Q8** (the modulus claim a student is asked to prove or disprove).]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** *A counterexample needs the hypothesis true and the conclusion false — check both halves every
time.*

| | $a\mid bc$? | $a\mid b$? | $a\mid c$? | counterexample? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | $5\mid200$ ✓ | $5\mid10$ ✓ | — | **no** — the conclusion holds |
| II | $8\mid16$ ✓ | $8\mid4$ ✗ | $8\mid4$ ✗ | **yes** |
| III | $6\mid84$ ✓ | $6\mid7$ ✗ | $6\mid12$ ✓ | **no** — the conclusion holds |

$$\boxed{\text{II only}}$$

*I and III are the two standard distractors: in I the hypothesis holds and so does the conclusion; in III
one disjunct fails, which is not enough, because "or" needs **both** to fail.*

**(b)** The claim becomes true when $a$ is **prime** — this is $\boxed{\text{Euclid's lemma}}$. In II the
divisor $8$ is composite, and its factors of $2$ are shared out between $b$ and $c$.

**(c)** **True.** By Bézout there are integers $x,y$ with $ax+by=1$. Multiply by $c$:

$$acx+bcy=c .$$

*Now both terms on the left are multiples of $a$:* the first obviously, and the second because $a\mid bc$.
Hence $a\mid c$. $\blacksquare$

*This is the real content of Euclid's lemma — "$a$ prime" was only ever a convenient way of guaranteeing
$\gcd(a,b)=1$.*

**(d)** The correct statement is the **triangle inequality**

$$\boxed{\lvert a+b\rvert\le\lvert a\rvert+\lvert b\rvert}$$

Equality holds exactly when $a$ and $b$ do not point in opposite directions — that is, when $ab\ge0$: both
non-negative, both non-positive, or at least one of them zero. Strict inequality holds exactly when
$ab<0$.

*So the original claim fails on a very large set, not just at one point — any $a=b=1$ will do.*
:::

### S6 · Scrambled proofs

Anchor the ends, then follow the dependencies.

1. **First line** introduces notation or assumes the hypothesis ("Let…", "Suppose…").
2. **Last line** states the conclusion, or the contradiction.
3. A line can only come after every line it **uses**.
4. Connecting words carry the order: *therefore*, *hence*, *so*, *it follows*.

**Build the chain yourself before reading the options** — the distractors are a tidy but wrong parallel
chain, so comparing them directly is slower and riskier.

[rare: one TMUA question in eight years, 2016 P2 Q7]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
These five steps form a proof that, for non-zero real $a$ and $b$, the curve $y=x^{3}+ax^{2}+b$ has three
distinct real roots whenever

$$27b\left(b+\frac{4a^{3}}{27}\right)<0 .$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**P.** Therefore $y$ has a local maximum and a local minimum, with values $b$ and
$b+\tfrac{4a^{3}}{27}$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**Q.** Differentiating, $\tfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=3x^{2}+2ax=x(3x+2a)$, which vanishes at
$x=0$ and $x=-\tfrac{2a}{3}$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**R.** A cubic has three distinct real roots exactly when its two stationary values have
opposite signs.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**S.** The given inequality says precisely that $b$ and $b+\tfrac{4a^{3}}{27}$ have opposite
signs.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**T.** Hence the cubic has three distinct real roots.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Put the five steps in a correct order.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Verify the two stationary values quoted in **P**.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Which step silently needs $a\ne0$, and what goes wrong without it?
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** Is the condition also **necessary** for three distinct real roots?

[Adapted from **2022 P2 Q17**, where a student's version of exactly this proof must be assessed; the ordering, the $a=0$ gap and the converse are added here.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** $\boxed{\textbf{Q},\ \textbf{P},\ \textbf{R},\ \textbf{S},\ \textbf{T}}$ — differentiate, read off
the stationary values, quote the criterion, check the criterion, conclude. (Swapping **R** and **S** is
equally valid; nothing else is.)

**(b)** $y(0)=b$, and

$$y\!\left(-\tfrac{2a}{3}\right)=-\frac{8a^{3}}{27}+a\cdot\frac{4a^{2}}{9}+b
=-\frac{8a^{3}}{27}+\frac{12a^{3}}{27}+b=\frac{4a^{3}}{27}+b .\ ✓$$

**(c)** Step **P**. If $a=0$ then $\tfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=3x^{2}$, which is zero only at $x=0$ and
never changes sign:

$$\boxed{a=0\text{ gives one stationary point, a point of inflection — no maximum and no minimum.}}$$

The curve $y=x^{3}+b$ is strictly increasing and has exactly **one** real root for every $b$, so the whole
argument collapses. *Step Q is still correct at $a=0$; it is the move from "two stationary points" to "a
maximum and a minimum" that needs the two to be distinct.*

**(d)** **Yes.** Every link in the chain is reversible: three distinct real roots force the two stationary
values to have strictly opposite signs, hence a negative product, hence the inequality. So

$$\boxed{\text{the condition is necessary and sufficient, not merely sufficient.}}$$

*The exam asks only for "if", which is a hint worth distrusting — check whether the stronger "if and only
if" is available, because a later part often needs it.*
:::

### S7 · The 20-second error scan ★

1. **Name the target:** write the claim as $P\Rightarrow Q$.
2. **Check the ends:** does the proof start from $P$ and reach $Q$ — or has it proved the converse?
3. **Read one arrow at a time:** ask, *"Does this follow for every value still allowed?"*
4. **Stop at the first false claim**, not the final absurdity it causes.
5. **Stress-test the boundary:** try $0$, $1$, equality, the smallest case, and any excluded endpoint.

Every line may be true but the **link** between two lines can still fail. A one-way step is not an error if
it is stated only as a necessary condition; the error comes when it is treated as reversible.

[do not force an error — sometimes the whole argument is valid]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**A.** $\sin^{2}x+\cos^{2}x=1$ for all values of $x$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B.** Therefore $\cos x=\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}x}$ for all values of $x$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C.** Hence $1+\cos x=1+\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}x}$ for all values of $x$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D.** Thus $(1+\cos x)^{2}=\left(1+\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}x}\right)^{2}$ for all values of $x$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**E.** Substituting $x=\pi$ gives $0=4$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** On which line does the first error occur?
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Give the complete set of $x$ in $[0,2\pi]$ for which that line is in fact valid.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Repair the line, and show that line **E** then produces no contradiction.

[Adapted from **2021 P2 Q5**, which asks only for the offending line; parts (b) and (c) are added.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** $\boxed{\textbf{B}}$.

*The square root symbol denotes the **non-negative** root,* so $\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}x}=\lvert\cos x\rvert$, not
$\cos x$. Line A is a genuine identity; lines C, D and E are all legitimate consequences of B — adding $1$
and squaring are valid operations. The falsehood is injected at B and merely carried along.

**(b)** Line B asserts $\cos x=\lvert\cos x\rvert$, which holds exactly when $\cos x\ge0$:

$$\boxed{\left[0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\cup\left[\tfrac{3\pi}{2},\,2\pi\right]}$$

**(c)** The correct statement is

$$\lvert\cos x\rvert=\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}x},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \cos x=\pm\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}x}.$$

At $x=\pi$ the correct sign is the negative one, so $\cos\pi=-\sqrt{1-0}=-1$. Line C then reads
$1+(-1)=0$ and line D reads $0^{2}=0^{2}$:

$$\boxed{0=0\ \text{— no contradiction.}}$$

*The absurd conclusion was not caused by the squaring, which is where the eye is drawn. Scan for the step
that quietly discarded a sign.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::
::: {.fs-card}
### S7 · High-risk moves ★

| If you see… | Check immediately… |
|---|---|
| **cancel / divide** | Can the divisor be $0$? Factor and split cases instead. |
| **square / root** | Squaring may add roots; $\sqrt{u^2}=\lvert u\rvert$; check candidates in the original. |
| **inequality** | Is the sign known? Negative multipliers and decreasing functions reverse the sign; $0<a<1$ makes $\log_a$ decreasing. |
| **inverse or trig step** | Is the function one-to-one on the stated domain? $\sin A=\sin B\not\Rightarrow A=B$. |
| **theorem or implication** | Are all hypotheses met, and is the arrow being used in the stated direction? |
| **"for all" claim** | One valid counterexample destroys it; test exceptional and boundary cases. |

**Wording controls equivalence.** "Is equivalent to" demands both directions. "Any solution must satisfy"
claims only one direction; those values are **candidates**, not solutions, until checked.

[full notes: **[S7 notes](../toolkit/s07_spot_the_error.qmd)** · **[S7 extended](../toolkit/s07_extended_equivalence.qmd)**]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Solve $4x\sqrt{2x-1}=10x-5$ completely. A student divides both sides by
$\sqrt{2x-1}$ — which solution does that lose, and why?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** A student solves $x^{4}-2x^{2}-3<0$ like this:

$$x^{4}-2x^{2}-3<0\ \iff\ x^{4}-2x^{2}+1<4\ \iff\ \left(x^{2}-1\right)^{2}<4\ \iff\ x^{2}-1<2 .$$

Solve the inequality correctly. The student's final answer is right — so what exactly is wrong with the last
step, and why does it not bite here?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Now solve $\left(x^{2}-5\right)^{2}<4$, and show that the same slip would give the wrong
answer.

[Adapted from **2018 P2 Q9** (the $4x\sqrt{2x-1}=10x-5$ manipulation) and **2023 P2 Q10** (the completing-the-square attempt at a quartic inequality).]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** *Substitute rather than divide.* Put $t=\sqrt{2x-1}\ge0$, so $x=\tfrac{t^{2}+1}{2}$ and the right
side is $5(2x-1)=5t^{2}$:

$$4\cdot\frac{t^{2}+1}{2}\cdot t=5t^{2}\ \Longrightarrow\ 2t^{3}-5t^{2}+2t=0\ \Longrightarrow\
t\left(2t-1\right)\left(t-2\right)=0 .$$

So $t=0,\tfrac12,2$, giving $2x-1=0,\tfrac14,4$ and

$$\boxed{x=\tfrac12,\ \tfrac58,\ \tfrac52}$$

*(All three check in the original equation.)* Dividing by $\sqrt{2x-1}$ throws away $\boxed{x=\tfrac12}$,
because at that value the divisor is **zero** — and dividing by zero is not a reversible step.

**(b)** Correctly: put $u=x^{2}$, so $u^{2}-2u-3<0$, i.e. $(u-3)(u+1)<0$, i.e. $-1<u<3$. Since
$u=x^{2}\ge0$ this means $0\le x^{2}<3$:

$$\boxed{-\sqrt3<x<\sqrt3}$$

The faulty step is $\left(x^{2}-1\right)^{2}<4\iff x^{2}-1<2$. *Squaring is not order-preserving on the
negatives,* so the right statement is

$$\left(x^{2}-1\right)^{2}<4\iff\left\lvert x^{2}-1\right\rvert<2\iff-2<x^{2}-1<2 .$$

The student kept only the upper half and dropped $x^{2}-1>-2$. It does not bite because that half says
$x^{2}>-1$, which is **automatic** for real $x$ — a vacuous condition. *A right answer from a wrong step.*

**(c)** $\left(x^{2}-5\right)^{2}<4\iff-2<x^{2}-5<2\iff3<x^{2}<7$, so

$$\boxed{-\sqrt7<x<-\sqrt3\ \text{ or }\ \sqrt3<x<\sqrt7}$$

Keeping only $x^{2}-5<2$ would give $-\sqrt7<x<\sqrt7$, wrongly including everything between $-\sqrt3$ and
$\sqrt3$ — for instance $x=0$, where $\left(0-5\right)^{2}=25$ is nowhere near less than $4$.

*Here the lower bound $x^{2}>3$ is a real restriction, so the same slip is fatal. Whether a dropped
inequality matters depends on the numbers, which is exactly why you must not drop it.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

## Equivalence, necessary and sufficient conditions {#s2-check}

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · One arrow or two?</div>
<div class="fs-title">Equivalent means exactly the same cases</div>
<div class="fs-sub">Track both the logical direction and the domain. A valid one-way step produces a necessary condition; it does not automatically produce an equivalent statement.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Equivalent = both directions

$$A\Leftrightarrow B
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(A\Rightarrow B)\text{ and }(B\Rightarrow A).$$

Across the stated domain, $A$ and $B$ must be true in **exactly the same cases**. For equations or
inequalities, this means the **same solution set**: no gained solutions and no lost solutions.

| known | correct description |
|---|---|
| $A\Leftrightarrow B$ | each is necessary **and** sufficient for the other |
| $A\Rightarrow B$ only | $A$ is sufficient for $B$; $B$ is necessary for $A$ |
| $B\Rightarrow A$ only | $B$ is sufficient for $A$; $A$ is necessary for $B$ |

[tail = sufficient; head = necessary]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Find a **necessary and sufficient** condition on the real numbers $b$ and $c$ for
$x^{4}+bx^{2}+c=0$ to have four distinct real roots.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Show that $b^{2}>4c$ on its own is necessary but **not** sufficient, and that
"$c>0$ and $b<0$" on its own is also necessary but not sufficient.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** How many distinct real roots are there when $c>0$ and $b=-2\sqrt c$?

[Adapted from **2023 P2 Q18**, which asks for the condition alone; the failure modes and the boundary case are added.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** *Substitute $u=x^{2}$, but remember that each $u$ gives two values of $x$ only when $u>0$.*
Four distinct real $x$ requires $u^{2}+bu+c=0$ to have **two distinct positive** roots, so

$$b^{2}-4c>0,\qquad u_1+u_2=-b>0,\qquad u_1u_2=c>0 .$$

That is $c>0$, $b<0$ and $b^{2}>4c$. With $c>0$ the last two collapse into one:

$$\boxed{c>0\ \text{ and }\ b<-2\sqrt c}$$

**(b)** Each condition is necessary, being part of (a). Neither is sufficient:

| | satisfied by | distinct real roots |
|---|---|---|
| $b^{2}>4c$ only | $b=2,\ c=-3$ | $2$ — the $u$-roots are $1$ and $-3$, and the negative one gives nothing |
| $c>0,\ b<0$ only | $b=-5,\ c=7$ | $0$ — $b^{2}=25<28=4c$, so no real $u$ at all |

**(c)** Then $b^{2}=4c$ exactly, so $u^{2}+bu+c=\left(u-\sqrt c\right)^{2}$ has the single **repeated**
root $u=\sqrt c>0$, giving $x=\pm c^{1/4}$:

$$\boxed{2\text{ distinct real roots}}$$

*So the boundary $b=-2\sqrt c$ must be excluded, which is why the inequality in (a) is strict.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### A valid one-way step

Let $A:\sqrt{2x+3}=x$ and $B:2x+3=x^2$. Squaring proves

$$A\Rightarrow B,$$

so $B$ is **necessary for** $A$. But $x=-1$ satisfies $B$ and not $A$, so $B\not\Rightarrow A$.

The safe wording is:

> Any solution of $A$ **must satisfy** $B$; solve $B$, then check those candidates in $A$.

A one-way step can be valid. The error is calling it **equivalent**, or promoting unchecked candidates to
solutions.

[$A\Rightarrow B$ means $\operatorname{Sol}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{Sol}(B)$]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Solve $\sqrt{2x+3}=x$. Which of the two roots of the squared equation is genuine, and
which direction of implication does the squaring provide?
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Solve $\sqrt{x+4}-\sqrt{x-1}=1$, squaring twice. State the domain restriction before
you start.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** For each part, write the relation between $\operatorname{Sol}(A)$ and
$\operatorname{Sol}(B)$, where $A$ is the original equation and $B$ the squared one, and say which part
gained a false candidate.

[Adapted from **2018 P2 Q9**, where a similar surd equation is manipulated and a root is lost.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** Squaring gives $2x+3=x^{2}$, i.e. $x^{2}-2x-3=0$, so $x=3$ or $x=-1$.

*Check both in the original, because squaring only works forwards:*

$$x=3:\ \sqrt9=3\ ✓\qquad x=-1:\ \sqrt1=1\ne-1\ ✗$$

$$\boxed{x=3}$$

Squaring gives $A\Rightarrow B$ only: a square root is never negative, so $x=-1$ could never have been a
solution of $A$. *The squared equation is **necessary**, not equivalent.*

**(b)** The domain needs $x+4\ge0$ and $x-1\ge0$, so $\boxed{x\ge1}$. Rearrange before squaring, to keep one
surd on each side:

$$\sqrt{x+4}=1+\sqrt{x-1}\ \Longrightarrow\ x+4=1+2\sqrt{x-1}+x-1\ \Longrightarrow\ 2\sqrt{x-1}=4 .$$

So $\sqrt{x-1}=2$ and $x=5$. *Check:* $\sqrt9-\sqrt4=3-2=1$ ✓.

$$\boxed{x=5}$$

**(c)** In both parts $A\Rightarrow B$, hence
$\operatorname{Sol}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{Sol}(B)$.

- In (a) the inclusion is **strict**: $\operatorname{Sol}(B)=\{-1,3\}$ against $\operatorname{Sol}(A)=\{3\}$,
so squaring gained a false candidate.
- In (b) it happens to be an **equality**, $\{5\}=\{5\}$ — but that is a fact discovered by checking, not
something the squaring guaranteed.

*The safe wording is always "any solution must satisfy $B$": solve $B$, then test the candidates in $A$.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Equivalent statement $\neq$ negation

For $S:\ \forall n>1,\ P(n)\Rightarrow Q(n)$:

| asked for | result |
|---|---|
| **equivalent to $S$** | $\forall n>1,\ \lnot Q(n)\Rightarrow\lnot P(n)$ |
| **negation of $S$** | $\exists n>1,\ P(n)\wedge\lnot Q(n)$ |

The first is the **contrapositive**, so it has the same truth conditions as $S$. The second gives exactly
the counterexample that makes $S$ false.

The domain restriction $n>1$ stays fixed; it is not replaced by $n\le1$.

[equivalent: same truth · negation: opposite truth]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
For a positive integer $k$, let $(\ast)$ be the theorem

> if $2^{k}+1$ is prime, then $k$ is a power of $2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Which of these is **equivalent** to $(\ast)$? Justify each verdict.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I. If $k$ is a power of $2$, then $2^{k}+1$ is prime.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;II. $2^{k}+1$ is not prime only if $k$ is not a power of $2$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;III. A sufficient condition for $k$ to be a power of $2$ is that $2^{k}+1$ is prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Write the **negation** of $(\ast)$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Prove $(\ast)$ by proving its contrapositive.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** Give a value of $k$ showing that statement I is false.

[Adapted from **2023 P2 Q11**, which asks only which statements are equivalent; the negation, the proof and the counterexample to the converse are added.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Write $P$: "$2^{k}+1$ is prime" and $Q$: "$k$ is a power of $2$", so $(\ast)$ is $P\Rightarrow Q$.

**(a)**

| | symbolic form | name | equivalent? |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | $Q\Rightarrow P$ | converse | **no** |
| II | $\lnot P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$ | inverse | **no** |
| III | $P\Rightarrow Q$ | the statement itself | **yes** |

$$\boxed{\text{III only}}$$

*II is the trap.* "$\lnot P$ only if $\lnot Q$" puts $\lnot P$ at the tail, giving
$\lnot P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$ — the **inverse**. The contrapositive would be $\lnot Q\Rightarrow\lnot P$, with
the two sides the other way round.

**(b)** $$\boxed{\exists k\in\mathbb Z^{+}:\ 2^{k}+1\text{ is prime and }k\text{ is not a power of }2}$$

**(c)** Contrapositive: *if $k$ is not a power of $2$, then $2^{k}+1$ is not prime.*

If $k$ is not a power of $2$ it has an **odd** factor $d>1$; write $k=dm$. For odd $d$,

$$y+1\ \text{ divides }\ y^{d}+1 ,$$

since $y^{d}+1=(y+1)\left(y^{d-1}-y^{d-2}+\cdots+1\right)$. Put $y=2^{m}$:

$$2^{m}+1\ \text{ divides }\ 2^{dm}+1=2^{k}+1 .$$

*And the divisor is proper:* $1<2^{m}+1<2^{k}+1$ because $m<k$. So $2^{k}+1$ is composite. $\blacksquare$

**(d)** $\boxed{k=32}$, a power of $2$, yet

$$2^{32}+1=4294967297=641\times6700417 .$$

*Euler's factorisation. So the converse fails, which is exactly why $(\ast)$ is one-directional.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}

## Part 1 examples — high-frequency traps

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · S1–S7</div>
<div class="fs-title">Ten questions to check before the exam</div>
<div class="fs-sub">One question for each of S1–S7, plus three harder S4 checks from the dedicated clinic. Decide first; then read the check.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### S1 · Read the wording

Let $P$ mean “$n$ is divisible by $6$” and $Q$ mean “$n$ is divisible by $3$”. Which are equivalent to
$P\Rightarrow Q$?

1. $P$ **only if** $Q$.
2. $Q$ **if** $P$.
3. $P$ **if** $Q$.
4. $Q$ **only if** $P$.

**Check:** **1 and 2**. Statements 3 and 4 are the converse, $Q\Rightarrow P$; $n=3$ disproves it.

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
Let $x$ be a real number and consider the five statements

$$\textbf{A}:\ x\ge0\qquad \textbf{B}:\ x=1\qquad \textbf{C}:\ x=0\text{ or }x=1$$
$$\textbf{D}:\ x\ge0\text{ or }x\le1\qquad \textbf{E}:\ x\ge0\text{ and }x\le1$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Which one is a **sufficient** condition for exactly **three** of the other four?
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Which one is sufficient for **all** four of the others?
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Which one is **necessary** for all four of the others?

[Adapted from **2023 P2 Q13** (exactly these five statements); parts (b) and (c) are added.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

*Turn each statement into its solution set — "sufficient" then means "is a subset of".*

$$A=[0,\infty),\quad B=\{1\},\quad C=\{0,1\},\quad D=\mathbb R,\quad E=[0,1].$$

*$D$ is the whole line:* every real number is either $\ge0$ or $\le1$ — in fact numbers in $[0,1]$ are both.
Spotting that $D$ is vacuous is the key move.

| is a subset of $\to$ | $A$ | $B$ | $C$ | $D$ | $E$ | count |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $A=[0,\infty)$ | — | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | ✗ | 1 |
| $B=\{1\}$ | ✓ | — | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | **4** |
| $C=\{0,1\}$ | ✓ | ✗ | — | ✓ | ✓ | **3** |
| $D=\mathbb R$ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | — | ✗ | 0 |
| $E=[0,1]$ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | — | 2 |

**(a)** $\boxed{\textbf{C}}$ — sufficient for $A$, $D$ and $E$, but not for $B$ (since $x=0$ is allowed).

**(b)** $\boxed{\textbf{B}}$ — the smallest set, so it sits inside all the others.

**(c)** $\boxed{\textbf{D}}$ — "necessary for $Y$" means $Y$ is a subset of it, and $\mathbb R$ contains
everything.

*The smallest set is sufficient for the most; the largest set is necessary for the most. Reading the columns
instead of the rows answers (c) with no extra work.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S2 · Equivalent or negated?

For every integer $n>1$,

$$n^2\text{ even}\Rightarrow n\text{ even}.$$

Write (a) an equivalent statement and (b) its negation.

**Check:** (a) the contrapositive: *if $n$ is odd, then $n^2$ is odd*. (b) there exists an integer $n>1$
such that $n^2$ is even **and** $n$ is odd.

[swap-and-negate gives an equivalent; keep-and-deny gives the negation]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
Consider the claim

> the difference between two consecutive positive cube numbers is always prime.

A student argues: $(x+1)^{3}-x^{3}=3x^{2}+3x+1$; the discriminant of $3x^{2}+3x+1$ is negative, so it has no
linear factors with integer coefficients; therefore $3x^{2}+3x+1$ cannot be factorised; hence the difference
is always prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Write the negation of the claim.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Decide the claim, giving the smallest counterexample.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Identify the first faulty step in the student's argument and say exactly what is wrong
with it.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** Write the contrapositive of "if $3x^{2}+3x+1$ is prime then $x$ is not a multiple of
$5$", and decide whether it is true.

[Adapted from **2022 P2 Q7**, where the same claim and the same flawed proof are assessed.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** $$\boxed{\exists\text{ a positive integer }x:\ (x+1)^{3}-x^{3}\text{ is not prime}}$$

**(b)** The differences are $7,19,37,61,\mathbf{91},127,169,217,\dots$ and

$$\boxed{x=5:\quad 216-125=91=7\times13}$$

so the claim is **false**. *(Later failures: $x=7$ gives $169=13^{2}$ and $x=8$ gives $217=7\times31$.)*

**(c)** The step "**therefore $3x^{2}+3x+1$ cannot be factorised**" is the first faulty one.

*Irreducibility as a polynomial says nothing about the integer values it takes.* A polynomial with no
integer linear factors can still produce composite **numbers** — its value at a particular $x$ may factorise
in a way that has nothing to do with factorising the polynomial. At $x=5$ the value $91$ splits as
$7\times13$, while $3x^{2}+3x+1$ itself remains irreducible.

**(d)** Contrapositive: *if $x$ is a multiple of $5$, then $3x^{2}+3x+1$ is not prime.*

This is **false**: $x=10$ gives $3(100)+30+1=331$, which is prime. *Since a statement and its
contrapositive stand or fall together, the original implication is false too — $x=10$ refutes both.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S3 · Necessary means the larger set

For real $x$, let

$$A:x<2,\quad B:0<x<1,\quad C:x^2<1,$$
$$D:\lvert x-1\rvert<2,\quad E:x^2<4.$$

Which statement is necessary for **exactly three** of the other four?

**Check:** **$A$**. Its set $(-\infty,2)$ contains $B=(0,1)$, $C=(-1,1)$ and $E=(-2,2)$, but not
$D=(-1,3)$.

[Woonju dedicated clinic: draw the five intervals before counting]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
The line $ax+by=c$ is drawn, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are non-zero real constants. Let $T$ be the property

> the line has positive gradient **and** positive $y$-intercept.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Write the gradient and the $y$-intercept in terms of $a$, $b$, $c$, and hence give a
**necessary and sufficient** condition for $T$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Show that "$a$ and $c$ have opposite signs" is necessary but **not** sufficient for $T$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Show that "$a>b>c$" is **neither** necessary nor sufficient for $T$.

[Adapted from **2023 P2 Q7**, which asks for the necessary-but-not-sufficient option; here every option is classified.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** Since $b\ne0$ we may write $y=-\dfrac{a}{b}x+\dfrac{c}{b}$, so

$$\text{gradient}=-\frac{a}{b},\qquad y\text{-intercept}=\frac{c}{b}.$$

$$\boxed{T\iff \frac{a}{b}<0\ \text{ and }\ \frac{c}{b}>0}$$

**(b)** **Necessary.** If $T$ holds then $a$ and $b$ have opposite signs while $c$ and $b$ have the same
sign, so $a$ and $c$ have opposite signs.

**Not sufficient.** Take $a=-3$, $b=-3$, $c=1$: here $a$ and $c$ have opposite signs, but

$$\text{gradient}=-\frac{-3}{-3}=-1<0 .$$

$$\boxed{\text{necessary, not sufficient}}$$

*The condition says nothing about $b$, and the gradient and intercept both depend on $b$ — so information
about $a$ and $c$ alone can never be enough.*

**(c)** **Not sufficient:** $a=-1$, $b=-2$, $c=-3$ satisfies $-1>-2>-3$, yet the $y$-intercept is
$\tfrac{-3}{-2}=\tfrac32>0$ while the gradient is $-\tfrac{-1}{-2}=-\tfrac12<0$.

**Not necessary:** $a=-3$, $b=1$, $c=1$ gives gradient $3>0$ and $y$-intercept $1>0$, so $T$ holds — but
$-3>1$ is false.

$$\boxed{\text{neither}}$$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S4 · Quantifier order

Which statements are true?

1. $\forall x\in\mathbb R\ \forall n\in\mathbb Z^+:\ x<n$.
2. $\forall x\in\mathbb R\ \exists n\in\mathbb Z^+:\ x<n$.
3. $\exists x\in\mathbb R\ \forall n\in\mathbb Z^+:\ x<n$.

**Check:** **2 and 3**. In 2, choose an $n$ depending on $x$. In 3, one value such as $x=0$ works for
every positive integer $n$. Statement 1 fails at $x=100,n=1$.

[2022 Paper 2 trap: later variables may depend on earlier ones]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Find the complete set of real $k$ for which

$$(\ast)\quad \forall x\in\mathbb R:\ \ x<k\Rightarrow x^{2}<k$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;is true. Justify your answer.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Now restrict the variable: find the complete set of $k$ for which

$$(\ast\ast)\quad \forall x\ \text{with}\ 0<x<k:\ \ x^{2}<k$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;is true.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Write the negation of $(\ast)$ and use it to confirm your answer to (a).

[Adapted from **2022 P2 Q9** (the statement in part (a) verbatim) and the quantifier-order trio in **2022 P2 Q10**.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** $$\boxed{\text{no values of }k}$$

*The hypothesis $x<k$ is satisfied by arbitrarily negative $x$, and squaring makes those enormous.* Given
any $k$, choose

$$x=-\left(\lvert k\rvert+1\right).$$

Then $x<k$ certainly holds, while $x^{2}=\left(\lvert k\rvert+1\right)^{2}>\lvert k\rvert\ge k$. So
$(\ast)$ fails for **every** $k$.

**(b)** Now $x$ is squeezed into $(0,k)$, which is empty unless $k>0$. For $k>0$ the values of $x^{2}$ fill
$\left(0,k^{2}\right)$, so we need $k^{2}\le k$, i.e. $k\le1$:

$$\boxed{0<k\le1}$$

*Check the endpoint:* at $k=1$, $0<x<1$ gives $x^{2}<x<1$ ✓. At $k=1.5$, $x=1.4$ gives
$x^{2}=1.96>1.5$ ✗.

**(c)** $$\lnot(\ast)=\exists x\in\mathbb R:\ x<k\ \textbf{and}\ x^{2}\ge k .$$

*The implication becomes an "and" — never another implication.* Part (a) produced exactly such an $x$ for
every $k$, so the negation is true for all $k$ and $(\ast)$ is true for none. ✓

*The whole question turns on the **unstated domain** of $x$. Changing it from $\mathbb R$ to $(0,k)$ turns
"never" into a genuine interval.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S4+ · Negate through an implication

Negate

$$\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0\ \forall x:\quad
\lvert x-a\rvert<\delta\Rightarrow\lvert f(x)-f(a)\rvert<\varepsilon.$$

**Check:**

$$\exists\varepsilon>0\ \forall\delta>0\ \exists x:\quad
\lvert x-a\rvert<\delta\ \wedge\ \lvert f(x)-f(a)\rvert\ge\varepsilon.$$

Every quantifier flips in place, and $\lnot(P\Rightarrow Q)=P\wedge\lnot Q$ — the implication becomes
**and**, not another implication.

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
Let $u_1,u_2,u_3,\dots$ be a sequence of real numbers and $L$ a real number. Consider

$$S:\quad \forall\varepsilon>0\ \ \exists N\in\mathbb Z^{+}\ \ \forall n>N:\quad
\lvert u_n-L\rvert<\varepsilon .$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Write $\lnot S$, flipping every quantifier in place.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** For $u_n=(-1)^{n}$, prove that $\lnot S$ holds for **every** real $L$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Explain why the weaker statement
$\ \forall\varepsilon>0\ \forall N\ \exists n>N:\ \lvert u_n-L\rvert<\varepsilon$
is satisfied by $u_n=(-1)^{n}$ for two values of $L$, and say which.

[Adapted from the nested-quantifier negation in **2020 P2 Q6** and **2020 P2 Q13**, where conditions on a function must be sorted into necessary and sufficient.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** $$\boxed{\lnot S:\quad \exists\varepsilon>0\ \ \forall N\in\mathbb Z^{+}\ \ \exists n>N:\quad
\lvert u_n-L\rvert\ge\varepsilon}$$

*Each quantifier flips where it stands, and the final inequality is negated. There is no implication inside
here, but if there were, $\lnot(P\Rightarrow Q)$ would become $P\wedge\lnot Q$ — an "and", not an arrow.*

**(b)** Take $\varepsilon=1$. Let $N$ be any positive integer. Among $n=N+1$ and $n=N+2$ the terms $u_n$
take **both** values $+1$ and $-1$. Now

$$\lvert1-L\rvert+\lvert-1-L\rvert\ \ge\ \lvert(1-L)-(-1-L)\rvert=2 ,$$

so at least one of the two distances is $\ge1$. *Whatever $L$ is, it cannot be within $1$ of both $+1$ and
$-1$, because they are $2$ apart.* Hence some $n>N$ has $\lvert u_n-L\rvert\ge1$, which is exactly
$\lnot S$. $\blacksquare$

**(c)** The weaker statement only asks that $u_n$ comes within $\varepsilon$ of $L$ **infinitely often**,
not eventually always — the order $\forall N\,\exists n$ lets $n$ depend on $N$, so the sequence may wander
away again in between.

$$\boxed{L=1\ \text{ and }\ L=-1}$$

For $L=1$ every even $n$ gives $\lvert u_n-1\rvert=0<\varepsilon$, and there are even $n$ beyond every $N$;
similarly for $L=-1$ with odd $n$. No other $L$ works, since every term is at distance at least
$\min\left(\lvert1-L\rvert,\lvert1+L\rvert\right)>0$ from it.

*Moving one quantifier changes "converges to $L$" into "has a subsequence converging to $L$".*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S4+ · Negate $\forall\exists$

Negate:

> For every integer $n>1$, there exists a prime $p$ such that $p$ divides $n$.

**Check:** there exists an integer $n>1$ such that **every** prime $p$ fails to divide $n$:

$$\exists n>1\ \forall p\text{ prime}:\quad p\nmid n.$$

The original is true, so its negation is false. The condition $n>1$ is the **domain**, so it stays fixed:
the negation asks for a counterexample **inside the same domain**, not an unrelated value with $n\le1$.

[for a universal claim, its negation is the statement that a valid counterexample exists]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
Consider the statement

> every positive integer $N$ greater than $6$ can be written as the sum of two non-prime integers, each
> greater than $1$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Write the negation, keeping the domain restriction in place.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Which of $N=5$, $N=7$, $N=9$ are counterexamples? Give full reasons.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Find the next counterexample after those, and show that every **even** $N\ge8$ **can**
be written in the required form.

[Adapted from **2020 P2 Q4** (the statement and the three candidates verbatim); the domain trap is the point of the question.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** $$\boxed{\exists N>6:\ N\text{ cannot be written as a sum of two non-prime integers each }>1}$$

*The condition $N>6$ is the **domain**, so it stays. The negation hunts for a counterexample inside the same
domain — it does not become $N\le6$.*

**(b)**

| $N$ | in the domain? | all splits into two integers $>1$ | counterexample? |
|---|---|---|---|
| $5$ | **no** ($5\not>6$) | — | **no** |
| $7$ | yes | $2+5$, $3+4$ | **yes** — every split contains a prime |
| $9$ | yes | $2+7$, $3+6$, $4+5$ | **yes** — $2,7$ prime; $3$ prime; $5$ prime |

$$\boxed{N=7\text{ and }N=9\text{ only}}$$

*$N=5$ is the trap: it fails the property, but it is outside the range the statement claims anything about,
so it refutes nothing.*

**(c)** The next counterexample is $\boxed{N=11}$: the splits are $2+9,3+8,4+7,5+6$, and each contains a
prime.

For even $N\ge8$, write

$$N=4+(N-4).$$

Here $4$ is non-prime and greater than $1$; and $N-4$ is **even** and at least $4$, so it is non-prime and
greater than $1$ as well. $\blacksquare$

*So the statement is false, but only for small odd $N$ — $7$, $9$ and $11$. From $13=4+9$ onwards the odd
cases work too.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S4+ · Who may depend on whom?

Explain why

$$\forall x\in\mathbb R\ \exists y\in\mathbb R:\ x+y=0$$

is true, while $\exists y\in\mathbb R\ \forall x\in\mathbb R:\ x+y=0$ is false. Then negate both.

**Check:** in the first, choose $y=-x$; in the second, one fixed $y$ cannot work for every $x$.

$$\neg(\forall x\exists y:\ x+y=0)=\exists x\forall y:\ x+y\ne0,$$
$$\neg(\exists y\forall x:\ x+y=0)=\forall y\exists x:\ x+y\ne0.$$

[the later variable may depend on earlier choices; the earlier one cannot depend on later choices]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
Let $a_1,\dots,a_{100}$, $b_1,\dots,b_{100}$ and $c_1,\dots,c_{100}$ be integers with

$$a_n\ \ge\ b_n+c_n\qquad\text{for every }n .$$

Decide which of the following must be true, and refute the others.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I.** $\min a\ \ge\ \min b+\min c$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II.** $\max a\ \ge\ \max b+\max c$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III.** $\displaystyle\sum a_n\ \ge\ \sum b_n+\sum c_n$

[Adapted from **2022 P2 Q16**, where three sequences are related term by term and claims about their extremes must be judged.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**I is true.** For every $n$,

$$a_n\ \ge\ b_n+c_n\ \ge\ \min b+\min c ,$$

so **every** $a_n$ — in particular the smallest — is at least $\min b+\min c$. ✓

**III is true.** Add the $100$ given inequalities. ✓

**II is false.** *The maxima of $b$ and of $c$ need not occur at the same index, and the hypothesis only
links the three sequences index by index.* With two terms:

$$b=(10,\,0),\qquad c=(0,\,10),\qquad a=(10,\,10).$$

The hypothesis holds ($10\ge10$ twice), but

$$\max a=10,\qquad \max b+\max c=10+10=20 .$$

$$\boxed{\text{I and III only}}$$

*The asymmetry is the content of the question. For the minimum, the bound $\min b+\min c$ is available at
**every** index, so it survives; for the maximum, $\max b+\max c$ may be achieved at **no** index, so
nothing forces $a$ to reach it.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S5 · One counterexample is enough

A proof claims that the difference between consecutive positive cubes is always prime because

$$(x+1)^3-x^3=3x^2+3x+1$$

and this polynomial is irreducible over the integers. What breaks the proof?

**Check:** irreducible **polynomial** does not mean every integer **value** is prime. At $x=5$ the value is
$91=7\times13$. One counterexample disproves the universal claim.

[algebraic irreducibility $\neq$ numerical primality]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
The function $f$ is defined for all real $x$. Consider

$$(\ast)\qquad \int_{-5}^{0}f(x)\,\mathrm dx=\int_{0}^{5}f(x)\,\mathrm dx .$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Which of the following conditions are **necessary** for $(\ast)$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I. $f(x)=f(-x)$ on $[-5,5]$ &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
II. $f(x)=c$ on $[-5,5]$ &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
III. $f(x)=-f(-x)$ on $[-5,5]$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Exhibit a **single** $f$ satisfying $(\ast)$ that refutes all three at once.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Give a condition that is necessary **and** sufficient for $(\ast)$.

[Adapted from **2020 P2 Q6**, which asks only which conditions are necessary; the single refuting function and the exact condition are added.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** $\boxed{\text{none of them}}$.

*A condition is necessary only if it holds in **every** case where $(\ast)$ does, so one well-chosen $f$
kills it.* Conditions I and II are each *sufficient* — which is the distractor — and III is neither: an odd
$f$ gives $\int_{-5}^{0}f=-\int_{0}^{5}f$, which matches $(\ast)$ only when both sides are $0$.

**(b)** Take $$\boxed{f(x)=x^{2}+\sin\frac{2\pi x}{5}}.$$

The sine term has period $5$, so it integrates to $0$ over $[-5,0]$ and over $[0,5]$ alike, leaving

$$\int_{-5}^{0}f=\frac{125}{3}=\int_{0}^{5}f\ ✓$$

Yet $f$ is not even (the sine term), not odd (the $x^{2}$ term), and certainly not constant. One function,
three conditions refuted.

**(c)** Substituting $x\mapsto-x$ in the left-hand integral turns $(\ast)$ into
$\int_{0}^{5}f(-x)\,\mathrm dx=\int_{0}^{5}f(x)\,\mathrm dx$, i.e.

$$\boxed{\int_{0}^{5}\bigl(f(x)-f(-x)\bigr)\mathrm dx=0}$$

*In words: the **odd part** of $f$ must integrate to zero on $[0,5]$ — nothing at all is required of the even
part.* Conditions I and II force the odd part to vanish identically, which is far more than needed.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S6 · Start at the hypothesis

The task is to prove $H\Rightarrow C$. A student starts from $C$ and, through correct reversible algebra,
arrives at $H$. What has the written argument proved?

**Check:** as written, it proves the **converse** $C\Rightarrow H$. If every displayed step is explicitly an
equivalence, the chain may be reversed to prove the target — but the argument must say so or run from $H$ to
$C$.

[dedicated clinic: label the first line and last line before checking the middle]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
A student is asked to show that, for non-zero reals $a$ and $b$,

> if $a^{2}-4b^{3}\ge0$ then there exist real $x$ and $y$ with $a=xy(x+y)$ and $b=xy$.

The attempt reads:

&nbsp;&nbsp;(I) $(x-y)^{2}\ge0$ &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;(II) so $x^{2}+y^{2}-2xy\ge0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;(III) so $(x+y)^{2}-4xy\ge0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;(IV) so $x^{2}y^{2}(x+y)^{2}-4x^{3}y^{3}\ge0$ &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
(V) so $a^{2}-4b^{3}\ge0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Check each line for an algebraic error.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** What has the student actually proved? State it precisely.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Explain why reversing the written order would not repair the proof either, and identify
the one step that is genuinely not reversible.

[Adapted from **2021 P2 Q11**, which presents exactly this attempt and asks what is wrong with it.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** Every line is algebraically **correct**.

$(x+y)^{2}-4xy=x^{2}+2xy+y^{2}-4xy=x^{2}+y^{2}-2xy$, so (II) and (III) say the same thing; (IV) multiplies
(III) by $x^{2}y^{2}\ge0$, which preserves the inequality; and with $a=xy(x+y)$, $b=xy$ we have
$a^{2}=x^{2}y^{2}(x+y)^{2}$ and $4b^{3}=4x^{3}y^{3}$, giving (V).

**(b)** The argument begins by **assuming $x$ and $y$ exist** and ends at the hypothesis. So it proves

$$\boxed{\text{if such }x,y\text{ exist, then }a^{2}-4b^{3}\ge0}$$

— the **converse** of what was asked. *The question wanted the hypothesis as the starting point and the
existence as the destination; the student ran the road the other way.*

**(c)** Reading the lines bottom to top would require each "so" to reverse. Lines (V)$\to$(IV),
(III)$\to$(II)$\to$(I) are genuine equivalences, but

$$\boxed{\text{(III)}\Rightarrow\text{(IV)}\ \text{ is not reversible:}}$$

it multiplies by $x^{2}y^{2}$, and dividing back is illegal when $xy=0$. More fundamentally, the reversed
chain still starts from an expression **in $x$ and $y$**, so it never establishes that such $x$ and $y$ exist
— which is the whole content of the claim. *A proof of existence has to produce the objects.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S7 · Where equivalence first fails

A student solving

$$\log_2(3x-1)=1+2\log_2(x-1)$$

replaces $2\log_2(x-1)$ by $\log_2((x-1)^2)$ and later obtains $x=\tfrac12$ or $3$. Where is the first
error if every line claims equivalence?

**Check:** at the replacement. The original requires $x>1$, whereas $\log_2((x-1)^2)$ exists for $x\ne1$.
The widened domain admits the false root $x=\tfrac12$; only $x=3$ solves the original.

[same formula on the old domain; different equation on the larger domain]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
A student solves $\cos x+\sin x\tan x=2\sin x-1$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$:

&nbsp;&nbsp;(I) $\cos x-\sin x+\sin x\tan x-\sin x=-1$
&nbsp;&nbsp;(II) so $(\sin x-\cos x)(\tan x-1)=-1$
&nbsp;&nbsp;(III) so $\sin x-\cos x=-1$ or $\tan x-1=-1$
&nbsp;&nbsp;(IV) so $(\sin x-\cos x)^{2}=1$ or $\tan x=0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;(V) so $2\sin x\cos x=0$ or $\tan x=0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;(VI) so $x=0,\ \tfrac{\pi}{2},\ \pi,\ \tfrac{3\pi}{2},\ 2\pi$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Verify that lines (I) and (II) are correct.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** On which line does equivalence first fail, and why?
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Name a second place where equivalence is lost even if (III) were repaired.

[Adapted from **2019 P2 Q6**, which asks only for the first faulty line.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** Line (I) is the original rearranged: $\cos x+\sin x\tan x-2\sin x=-1$. ✓

For line (II), expand and use $\cos x\tan x=\sin x$:

$$(\sin x-\cos x)(\tan x-1)=\sin x\tan x-\sin x-\underbrace{\cos x\tan x}_{=\,\sin x}+\cos x
=\sin x\tan x-2\sin x+\cos x .\ ✓$$

**(b)** $\boxed{\text{Line (III)}}$.

*From $AB=-1$ it does not follow that $A=-1$ or $B=-1$.* That inference is only valid when the product is
**zero**, because a product vanishes exactly when a factor does. A product equal to $-1$ can be split in
infinitely many ways — $A=2,\,B=-\tfrac12$, for instance. The student has applied the zero-product rule to a
non-zero product.

**(c)** Line (III)$\to$(IV) squares $\sin x-\cos x=-1$ into $(\sin x-\cos x)^{2}=1$.

$$\boxed{\text{Squaring also admits }\sin x-\cos x=+1 ,}$$

so (IV) is strictly weaker than (III) and gains candidates. *Two separate failures of equivalence, each
pushing the answer in the direction of too many solutions — which is why every value in (VI) must be
substituted back into the original equation.*
:::

:::
