# Part 2 · T1 — Divisors and primes

*Fifteen-plus Paper 2 questions across 2016–2023, and **not one of them a calculation**. The mathematics is
tiny and repeats; learn it cold. Full page: **[T1](../toolkit/t01_divisors_primes.qmd)**.*

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · Topic T1</div>
<div class="fs-title">Divisors &amp; primes — the memorisable core</div>
<div class="fs-sub">Every card has a standard counterexample attached. Learn the counterexample with the fact — that is what the questions actually test.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Primes and the $6n\pm1$ form ★

Every prime $>3$ is of the form $6n\pm1$, because $6n$, $6n\pm2$ and $6n+3$ all carry a factor of $2$ or $3$.

**The converse is false:** $25$, $35$, $49$, $55$ are all $6n\pm1$ and none is prime.

**Edge cases that break proofs:** $1$ is **not** prime; $2$ is the **only** even prime; $3k$ is composite
**only when $k>1$**, since $3\times1=3$ is prime.

[$n^{2}+2$ is prime at $n=1$ — that single case kills several textbook "proofs"]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Prove that every prime greater than $3$ has the form $6n\pm1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Is the converse true? Give the two smallest counterexamples.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Find a counterexample to: *if $n$ is prime then $n^{2}+2$ is not prime.*
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** Prove that your counterexample is the **only** one.

[Adapted from **2017 P2 Q5** (statements about $10p^{2}\pm1$ and the $6n\pm1$ form) and **2022 P2 Q3** (a counterexample to the $n^{2}+2$ claim).]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** Every integer is $6n,6n\pm1,6n\pm2$ or $6n+3$. Of these, $6n$, $6n\pm2$ are even and $6n+3$ is a
multiple of $3$, so a prime bigger than $3$ can only be

$$\boxed{6n-1\ \text{ or }\ 6n+1}$$

*The argument discards four of the six residue classes on sight — that is why it is worth memorising rather
than re-deriving.*

**(b)** **No.** The form is necessary, not sufficient:

$$\boxed{25=6(4)+1,\qquad 35=6(6)-1}$$

both composite. *A classic distractor is to offer "$n$ has the form $6k\pm1$" as a sufficient condition for
primality.*

**(c)** $$\boxed{n=3:\quad 3^{2}+2=11,\ \text{which is prime}}$$

**(d)** Let $p$ be prime with $p>3$. By (a), $p\equiv\pm1\pmod 3$, so

$$p^{2}\equiv1\pmod 3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p^{2}+2\equiv0\pmod3 .$$

Since $p^{2}+2>3$, it is a proper multiple of $3$ and therefore composite. For the two small primes,
$p=2$ gives $6$ (composite) and $p=3$ gives $11$ (prime).

$$\boxed{n=3\text{ is the unique prime counterexample.}}$$

*Note how the $6n\pm1$ fact did the work: it fixed $p$ modulo $3$, and the whole question then collapsed to
one line of arithmetic.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Euclid's lemma — the missing word ★

**If $p$ divides $ab$, then $p$ divides $a$ or $p$ divides $b$** — *only if $p$ is prime.*

**Drop "prime" and it collapses:** $4$ divides $2\times2$ but $4$ does not divide $2$. Smallest
counterexample $a=4,\ b=c=2$.

[2016 P2 Q13 and 2021 P2 Q4 are the *same* false statement — this is the word they removed]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** State Euclid's lemma, underlining the word that cannot be dropped.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Find the **smallest** composite $a$, together with integers $b,c>1$, such that $a$
divides $bc$ but divides neither $b$ nor $c$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Prove: if $p$ is prime and $p\mid a^{n}$ for some $n\ge1$, then $p\mid a$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** Is it true that $a\mid b^{2}$ forces $a\mid b$? Decide, and give the smallest
counterexample if not.

[Adapted from **2021 P2 Q4**, whose counterexample $a=8,\ b=4,\ c=4$ is the same phenomenon one size larger.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** If a **prime** $p$ divides $bc$, then $p\mid b$ or $p\mid c$.

$$\boxed{\textbf{prime}\text{ is the word that cannot be dropped}}$$

**(b)** $$\boxed{a=4,\quad b=2,\quad c=2}$$

Here $bc=4$ is divisible by $4$, while $4\nmid2$. *The factor $2^{2}$ of $a$ is **split** between $b$ and
$c$, one copy each — which is exactly what primality rules out, since a prime has only one copy to give.*
No smaller composite exists, $4$ being the smallest composite number.

**(c)** Induct on $n$. For $n=1$ it is the statement itself. Suppose it holds for $n-1$ and let
$p\mid a^{n}=a\cdot a^{n-1}$. By Euclid's lemma, $p\mid a$ — in which case we are done — or
$p\mid a^{n-1}$, and then the inductive hypothesis gives $p\mid a$. $\blacksquare$

**(d)** **False.** $$\boxed{a=4,\ b=2:\quad 4\mid4\ \text{but}\ 4\nmid2}$$

*The implication $a\mid b^{2}\Rightarrow a\mid b$ holds exactly when $a$ is **squarefree** — see the card on
$m\mid n^{k}$. For $a=4$ the repeated prime is what breaks it.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Squaring doubles every exponent ★

$n=p_1^{e_1}p_2^{e_2}\cdots\Rightarrow n^{2}=p_1^{2e_1}p_2^{2e_2}\cdots$, so $n^{2}$ carries only **even**
powers.

For a **prime** $p$: if $p$ divides $n^{2}$ then $p$ divides $n$. For a composite divisor you only recover
its square root — **$12$ divides $n^{2}$ exactly when $6$ divides $n$**, *not* when $12$ divides $n$.

**Counterexample:** $n=6$ gives $n^{2}=36=12\times3$, yet $12$ does not divide $6$.

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Explain why every exponent in the prime factorisation of a perfect square is even, and
deduce that a perfect square has an **odd** number of divisors.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Find the smallest integer $n>1$ for which $2n$ is a perfect square **and** $3n$ is a
perfect cube.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Hence state, in terms of exponents, the condition for $kn$ to be a perfect $k$th power.

[Adapted from **2018 P2 Q17** ("squaresum" integers) and the exponent bookkeeping behind **2023 P2 Q16**.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** If $m=\prod p_i^{e_i}$ then $m^{2}=\prod p_i^{2e_i}$, so every exponent of a square is even.

The number of divisors is $\prod(2e_i+1)$ — *a product of odd numbers, hence odd.* Conversely an odd divisor
count forces every $e_i$ to be even, so

$$\boxed{\text{odd divisor count}\iff\text{perfect square}}$$

*The reason is that divisors pair up as $d$ with $m/d$, and only a square has a divisor paired with itself.*

**(b)** Only the primes $2$ and $3$ can appear, so write $n=2^{a}3^{b}$.

$$2n=2^{a+1}3^{b}\ \text{ a square}\ \Longrightarrow\ a+1\ \text{even},\ b\ \text{even}$$
$$3n=2^{a}3^{b+1}\ \text{ a cube}\ \Longrightarrow\ a\equiv0,\ b+1\equiv0 \pmod 3$$

So $a$ is **odd** and a multiple of $3$, giving $a=3$; and $b$ is **even** with $b\equiv2\pmod3$, giving
$b=2$:

$$\boxed{n=2^{3}\cdot3^{2}=72}$$

*Check:* $2n=144=12^{2}$ ✓ and $3n=216=6^{3}$ ✓.

**(c)** $kn$ is a perfect $k$th power exactly when, for every prime $p$,

$$\boxed{v_p(k)+v_p(n)\equiv0\pmod k}$$

where $v_p$ is the exponent of $p$. *Each prime is an independent congruence — which is why (b) reduced to
two tiny simultaneous conditions.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Remainders, and what squares leave

"$b$ leaves remainder $r$ on division by $a$" means $b=aq+r$ **with $0\le r<a$** — the size condition is
half the definition.

**Trap:** if $r,s<a$ the product $rs$ need **not** be $<a$, so $rs$ is not the remainder of $bc$. Take
$a=4$, $r=s=2$: $rs=4$, true remainder $0$.

$$n^{2}\equiv0,1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3)\qquad n^{2}\equiv0,1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)\qquad n^{2}\equiv0,1,4\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$$

A square is **never** $2\bmod3$ and **never** $3\bmod4$.

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** List the possible remainders of a perfect square modulo $3$, $4$, $5$ and $8$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Prove that $n^{2}+n+1$ is never divisible by $5$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Prove that no integer of the form $8k+7$ is a sum of **three** squares.

[Adapted from **2019 P2 Q7**, which uses $12^{2}+16^{2}=20^{2}$ to build a counterexample, and the residue arguments in **2018 P2 Q17**.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** *Only the residue of $n$ matters, so test one full set of residues.*

| modulus | possible residues of $n^{2}$ |
|---|---|
| $3$ | $0,1$ |
| $4$ | $0,1$ |
| $5$ | $0,1,4$ |
| $8$ | $0,1,4$ |

*Mod $8$ needs $n=0,\dots,7$ and gives only three values — the single most useful fact in this family.*

**(b)** Work modulo $5$ and test $n\equiv0,1,2,3,4$:

| $n$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $n^{2}+n+1$ | $1$ | $3$ | $2$ | $3$ | $1$ |

The value $0$ never appears, so $\boxed{5\nmid n^{2}+n+1\text{ for every integer }n}$.

*Five cases, five lines — a finite check settles a statement about infinitely many $n$.*

**(c)** By (a), each square is $0$, $1$ or $4$ modulo $8$. The possible sums of three such values are

$$\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6\}\pmod 8 ,$$

obtained by adding three elements of $\{0,1,4\}$ in all $10$ combinations. *The residue $7$ is the one that
never occurs.* Hence

$$\boxed{8k+7\text{ is never a sum of three squares.}}$$

*(This is sharp: every other residue class does contain sums of three squares.)*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Squares modulo 4 — what a sum of two squares can be ★

Every square is $0$ or $1$ modulo $4$, so

$$a^{2}+b^{2}\equiv 0,\ 1\ \text{or}\ 2 \pmod 4 \quad\text{— never } 3 .$$

**So no integer of the form $4k+3$ is a sum of two squares.** One residue check replaces a search.

Companion facts: a square is never $\equiv2\pmod 3$ and never $\equiv3\pmod 4$; and modulo $8$ a square is $0$, $1$ or $4$.

[$255=4(63)+3$, so it is not $a^{2}+b^{2}$ — no trial needed]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Prove that no integer of the form $4k+3$ is a sum of two squares.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Decide whether $2019$ is a sum of two squares, with reasons.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Prove that if $m$ and $n$ are each a sum of two squares, then so is $mn$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** Does the converse of (c) hold? Justify with the smallest example you can find.

[Adapted from **2018 P2 Q17**, which defines a "squaresum" and asks which integers are one.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** Modulo $4$ every square is $0$ or $1$, so a sum of two squares is

$$0+0,\ 0+1,\ 1+1\ \equiv\ 0,\ 1,\ 2\pmod4 .$$

$$\boxed{3\text{ is unreachable, so no }4k+3\text{ is a sum of two squares.}}$$

**(b)** $2019=4(504)+3$, so by (a)

$$\boxed{2019\text{ is not a sum of two squares}}$$

*One residue check replaces a search through $45$ candidate squares.*

**(c)** Write $m=a^{2}+b^{2}$ and $n=c^{2}+d^{2}$. Then

$$\boxed{(a^{2}+b^{2})(c^{2}+d^{2})=(ac-bd)^{2}+(ad+bc)^{2}}$$

*(expand both sides: the cross terms $-2abcd$ and $+2abcd$ cancel).* So $mn$ is a sum of two squares.
$\blacksquare$

*For example $5\times25=125=5^{2}+10^{2}$, via $a,b,c,d=1,2,3,4$.*

**(d)** **No.** Take

$$\boxed{m=3,\quad n=3,\quad mn=9=3^{2}+0^{2}}$$

$mn$ is a sum of two squares, yet $3$ is of the form $4k+3$ and so by (a) is not. *The product can "repair"
a bad factor only when the bad factor appears an even number of times — which is the start of the full
characterisation: $N$ is a sum of two squares exactly when every prime $\equiv3\pmod4$ occurs to an even
power.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Digit sums — why the tests work ★

Since $10\equiv1\pmod 9$, every power of $10$ is $\equiv1$, so for the digit sum $s(N)$

$$N\equiv s(N)\pmod 9,\qquad\text{hence } 9\mid N\iff 9\mid s(N),$$

and the same argument modulo $3$ gives the test for $3$. Modulo $11$, $10\equiv-1$, so the **alternating**
digit sum is what matters.

[$3\mid s(N)$ is necessary but **not** sufficient for $9\mid N$ — take $N=12$]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Prove the test for $9$: an integer $N$ is divisible by $9$ exactly when its digit sum
is.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Derive the corresponding test for $11$, stating clearly what replaces the digit sum.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Prove that $10^{n}+1$ is divisible by $11$ exactly when $n$ is odd, and hence write
down a composite number consisting of a $1$, some zeros and another $1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** Is "the digit sum of $N$ is divisible by $3$" sufficient for $9\mid N$?

[Adapted from **2023 P2 Q15**, which sets up base-$2$ place value and asks for an analogous divisibility argument.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** Since $10\equiv1\pmod9$, every power $10^{k}\equiv1$. So for $N=\sum d_k10^{k}$,

$$N\equiv\sum d_k\cdot1=s(N)\pmod9 ,$$

and $N$ and $s(N)$ leave the **same** remainder. In particular one is divisible by $9$ exactly when the
other is. $\blacksquare$

**(b)** Modulo $11$ we have $10\equiv-1$, so $10^{k}\equiv(-1)^{k}$ and

$$N\equiv d_0-d_1+d_2-d_3+\cdots\pmod{11}.$$

$$\boxed{\text{the }\textbf{alternating}\text{ digit sum replaces the digit sum}}$$

**(c)** $10^{n}+1\equiv(-1)^{n}+1\pmod{11}$, which is $0$ when $n$ is odd and $2$ when $n$ is even:

$$\boxed{11\mid10^{n}+1\iff n\text{ odd}}$$

Taking $n=3$ gives $\boxed{1001=11\times91=7\times11\times13}$. *(Taking $n=2$ gives $101$, which is prime —
so the parity of $n$ genuinely decides it.)*

**(d)** **No.** $$\boxed{N=12:\ s(N)=3\text{ is divisible by }3,\text{ but }9\nmid12}$$

*The congruence $N\equiv s(N)\pmod 9$ gives the test for $9$ **and** for $3$, because $3\mid9$ — but the
tests are not interchangeable. "Digit sum divisible by $3$" is necessary for $9\mid N$, never sufficient.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### When does $m\mid n^{k}$ force $m\mid n$? ★

Cubing **triples every exponent** in the prime factorisation, so the condition is about **repeated** primes,
not about being composite:

| $m$ | $m\mid n^{3}\Rightarrow m\mid n$? | |
|---|---|---|
| $2$, $3$, $p$ prime | **yes** | Euclid's lemma |
| $6=2\times3$ | **yes** | distinct primes, each to the power $1$ |
| $8=2^{3}$ | no | $n=2$ |
| $9=3^{2}$ | no | $n=3$ |

**$m$ works exactly when $m$ is squarefree** — no prime appears twice.

[composite is not the test: $6$ works and $8$ does not]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** For which $m$ in the range $2\le m\le12$ is it true that $m\mid n^{3}\Rightarrow m\mid n$
for **every** positive integer $n$? Give a counterexample for each failure.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Characterise the integers $m$ with that property, and prove your characterisation.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Does replacing $n^{3}$ by $n^{2}$ change the answer?

[Adapted from **2021 P2 Q4**, which asks for counterexamples to the $k=1$ version; the characterisation is the generalisation.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)**

| $m$ | works? | counterexample |
|---|---|---|
| $2,3,5,7,11$ | **yes** | — (prime) |
| $6,10$ | **yes** | — (distinct primes) |
| $4$ | no | $n=2$: $4\mid8$, $4\nmid2$ |
| $8$ | no | $n=2$: $8\mid8$, $8\nmid2$ |
| $9$ | no | $n=3$: $9\mid27$, $9\nmid3$ |
| $12$ | no | $n=6$: $12\mid216$, $12\nmid6$ |

$$\boxed{m=2,3,5,6,7,10,11}$$

**(b)** $$\boxed{\text{exactly the }\textbf{squarefree}\ m\text{ — no repeated prime factor}}$$

*Forwards.* Let $m=p_1p_2\cdots p_r$ with distinct primes and suppose $m\mid n^{3}$. Each $p_i$ divides
$n^{3}$, so by Euclid's lemma $p_i\mid n$. The $p_i$ are distinct, so their product divides $n$. ✓

*Backwards.* If $p^{2}\mid m$, write $m=p^{2}t$ and take $n=pt$. Then
$n^{3}=p^{3}t^{3}=m\cdot pt^{2}$, so $m\mid n^{3}$; but $m=p^{2}t$ does not divide $n=pt$, since that would
need $p\mid1$. ✓

**(c)** **No** — the characterisation is the same for every exponent $k\ge2$. *Cubing triples each exponent
and squaring doubles it, but either way one copy of a repeated prime can be hidden inside $n$ and still
produce enough copies in $n^{k}$.* Taking $k=2$: $m=4$, $n=2$ gives $4\mid4$ and $4\nmid2$ exactly as
before.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The gcd toolkit

Let $d=\gcd(a,b)$. This means $d$ is the greatest positive integer dividing **both** $a$ and $b$.
Therefore $a=dr$ and $b=ds$ for some integers $r,s$, so $d$ also divides every integer combination
$xa+yb$ — in particular, $a+b$ and $a-b$.

$$\gcd(a,\,b+ka)=\gcd(a,b)\qquad \gcd(n,\,n+1)=1$$

**Why this matters for a recurrence.** Suppose

$$u_1=a,\qquad u_2=b,\qquad u_{n+2}=u_n+u_{n+1}.$$

If $d$ divides both starting terms, then it divides $u_3=a+b$. It then divides
$u_4=b+u_3$, and the same argument repeats, so $d$ divides **every** term.

Also, the gcd of consecutive terms stays unchanged:

$$\gcd(u_{n+1},u_{n+2})
=\gcd(u_{n+1},u_n+u_{n+1})
=\gcd(u_n,u_{n+1}).$$

[example: $u_1=14,u_2=21$ gives $14,21,35,56,91,\ldots$; every term is divisible by $7$, and each consecutive gcd is $7$]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
A sequence is defined by $u_1=a$, $u_2=b$ and $u_{n+2}=u_n+u_{n+1}$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive
integers with $\gcd(a,b)=h$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Prove that $\gcd(u_n,u_{n+1})=h$ for every $n$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Deduce the highest common factor of $u_{10}$ and $u_{11}$ when $a=10$ and $b=15$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Use the Euclidean algorithm to evaluate $\gcd\!\left(2^{12}-1,\ 2^{18}-1\right)$, and
state the general rule it illustrates.

[Adapted from **2023 P2 Q16**, where exactly this recurrence appears and the highest common factor of consecutive terms is the subject.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** *The recurrence is a single step of the Euclidean algorithm run backwards.* For any $n$,

$$\gcd(u_{n+1},u_{n+2})=\gcd(u_{n+1},\,u_n+u_{n+1})=\gcd(u_{n+1},u_n),$$

since adding a multiple of one argument to the other never changes a gcd. So the gcd of consecutive terms is
**invariant**, and equals its value at the start:

$$\boxed{\gcd(u_n,u_{n+1})=\gcd(a,b)=h}$$

**(b)** By (a) the answer is immediate, with no need to compute the terms:

$$\boxed{\gcd(u_{10},u_{11})=\gcd(10,15)=5}$$

**(c)** $2^{12}-1=4095$ and $2^{18}-1=262143$. Running the algorithm,

$$262143=64\times4095+63,\qquad 4095=65\times63+0,$$

so $\boxed{\gcd=63}$. *Check:* $4095=3^{2}\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13$ and $262143=3^{3}\cdot7\cdot19\cdot73$,
sharing $3^{2}\cdot7=63$ ✓.

The general rule is

$$\boxed{\gcd\!\left(2^{m}-1,\ 2^{n}-1\right)=2^{\gcd(m,n)}-1}$$

and here $\gcd(12,18)=6$ with $2^{6}-1=63$. *An invariant turns a question about huge numbers into a
question about their exponents.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Irreducible $\neq$ prime-valued ★

A polynomial **factorises over the integers** if it can be written as

$$P(x)=A(x)B(x),$$

where $A$ and $B$ are non-constant polynomials whose **every coefficient — including each constant term —
is an integer**. If no such factorisation exists, $P$ is *irreducible over the integers*.

This does **not** mean “it cannot factor over the reals”: for example,
$x^2-2=(x-\sqrt2)(x+\sqrt2)$ over the reals, but not over the integers.

Irreducibility describes the polynomial as an algebraic expression; it does not guarantee that the integer
$P(n)$ is prime.

$3x^{2}+3x+1$ is irreducible ($D=9-12=-3<0$), yet $x=5$ gives $91=7\times13$ — which is exactly
$6^{3}-5^{3}$.

In fact, no non-constant polynomial in $\mathbb Z[x]$ gives a prime for **every** integer input. For TMUA,
you do not need the general proof: one composite output is enough to disprove an “always prime” claim.

**Two different meanings of “factor”:** 

- **integer factor:** $91=7\times13$, so $7$ and $13$ divide the number $91$;
- **polynomial factor:** $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$ as an identity in $x$.

An irreducible polynomial can therefore produce a composite integer. Treating these two meanings as the
same is the error.

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Verify that $n^{2}+n+41$ is prime for $n=0,1,2$, and find the smallest $n\ge0$ for
which it is **not**.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Prove that $n^{4}+4$ is composite for every integer $n>1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Prove that **no** non-constant polynomial with integer coefficients takes a prime value
at every positive integer.

[Adapted from **2022 P2 Q7**, where a student mistakes an irreducible quadratic for a prime-generating one, and **2018 P2 Q12**.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** $n=0,1,2$ give $41$, $43$, $47$ — all prime. The polynomial keeps producing primes for a
remarkably long time, and then

$$\boxed{n=40:\quad 40^{2}+40+41=1681=41^{2}}$$

*Visible in hindsight: at $n=41$ every term is a multiple of $41$, and at $n=40$ the expression is
$40\cdot41+41=41\cdot41$.*

**(b)** *Complete the square and factorise as a difference of two squares.*

$$n^{4}+4=\left(n^{4}+4n^{2}+4\right)-4n^{2}=\left(n^{2}+2\right)^{2}-(2n)^{2}$$
$$=\boxed{\left(n^{2}-2n+2\right)\left(n^{2}+2n+2\right)}$$

For $n>1$ the smaller factor is $n^{2}-2n+2=(n-1)^{2}+1\ge2$, so both factors exceed $1$ and the number is
composite. *(At $n=1$ the first factor is $1$, and indeed $5$ is prime — so the restriction $n>1$ is
exactly right.)*

**(c)** Let $f$ be non-constant with integer coefficients and suppose $f(1)=p$ is prime. For every integer
$k$,

$$f(1+kp)\equiv f(1)=p\equiv0\pmod p ,$$

because $f(1+kp)-f(1)$ is divisible by $(1+kp)-1=kp$. So $p$ divides $f(1+kp)$ for **every** $k$. Since $f$
is non-constant, $\lvert f(1+kp)\rvert>p$ for all large $k$, and such a value is a proper multiple of $p$ —
hence composite. $\blacksquare$

*So the pattern in (a) was always going to break. Irreducibility of a polynomial and primality of its values
are unrelated properties.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::::

:::::

::: {.callout-tip}
## The two reflexes for this topic

1. **Test $n=1,2,3,4$ before reasoning.** For $n^{3}+5n$ that gives $6,18,42,84$ — one line of arithmetic
   that eliminates five of seven options.
2. **Check the smallest allowed case of every "therefore it is composite" step.** Almost every flawed proof
   in this topic is correct for large $n$ and dies at the boundary.
:::

# Part 3 · T2 — Shapes as logical conditions

*Eight sittings, eight appearances. The geometry never goes beyond GCSE; what is tested is which property
forces which, and whether you can produce the standard counterexample on demand. Full page:
**[T2](../toolkit/t02_shapes_as_logic.qmd)**.*

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · Topic T2</div>
<div class="fs-title">Shapes as logical conditions</div>
<div class="fs-sub">The lattice, the diagonal table, the congruence criteria and the three counterexamples. Learn the <strong>arrows</strong>: every question here is asking you to read one off, usually backwards.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### The quadrilateral lattice ★

$$\text{square}\Rightarrow\text{rhombus}\Rightarrow\text{parallelogram}\Rightarrow\text{trapezium}$$
$$\text{square}\Rightarrow\text{rectangle}\Rightarrow\text{parallelogram}$$

A square is **both** a rhombus and a rectangle; nothing else is. A **kite** sits outside the chain unless it
is a rhombus.

*Arrows run one way only* — reading one backwards is what every wrong option in this topic does.

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
$PQRS$ is a quadrilateral labelled anticlockwise. Classify each condition as **sufficient but not
necessary**, **necessary but not sufficient**, **both**, or **neither** for $PQRS$ to be a parallelogram,
giving a counterexample for every "not".

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** $PQ=SR$ and $PS$ is parallel to $QR$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** $PQ=SR$ and $PQ$ is parallel to $SR$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** $PQ=QR=SR=SP$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** $PR=QS$.

[Adapted from **2019 P2 Q10**, which asks only which option is necessary but not sufficient; here all four are classified.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

*One shape settles three of the four parts.* Take the isosceles trapezium

$$P(1,2),\quad Q(0,0),\quad R(6,0),\quad S(5,2).$$

Here $PS$ and $QR$ are both horizontal, so they are parallel; the legs are
$PQ=SR=\sqrt5$; the diagonals are $PR=QS=\sqrt{29}$; and it is **not** a parallelogram, since
$\vec p+\vec r=(7,2)$ while $\vec q+\vec s=(5,2)$.

**(a) Necessary but not sufficient.** A parallelogram has both properties, so the condition is necessary.
The trapezium above satisfies it without being a parallelogram.

$$\boxed{\text{necessary, not sufficient}}$$

*This is the classic near-miss: one pair of sides **equal** and the **other** pair parallel. Equal and
parallel must be the **same** pair.*

**(b) Both.** One pair of opposite sides equal **and** parallel forces a parallelogram — and a
parallelogram has it. $\boxed{\text{necessary and sufficient}}$

**(c) Sufficient but not necessary.** Four equal sides make a rhombus, which is a parallelogram. But
$P(0,0),Q(4,0),R(5,2),S(1,2)$ is a parallelogram with unequal adjacent sides.

$$\boxed{\text{sufficient, not necessary}}$$

**(d) Neither.** Not sufficient — the trapezium has $PR=QS=\sqrt{29}$. Not necessary — the parallelogram
$P(0,0),Q(4,0),R(5,2),S(1,2)$ has $PR=\sqrt{29}$ and $QS=\sqrt{13}$.

$$\boxed{\text{neither}}$$

*Equal diagonals characterise a **rectangle** among parallelograms, not a parallelogram among
quadrilaterals.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The three counterexamples ★

- **rhombus** — equal sides, perpendicular diagonals, **not a square**
- **rectangle** — equal diagonals, right angles, **not a square**
- **isosceles trapezium** — one pair parallel, other pair equal, **not a parallelogram**

Almost every "is this sufficient?" question is killed by one of these three. *Reach for a named shape
before you try to prove anything.*

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
The two diagonals of the quadrilateral $Q$ are perpendicular. Consider

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I.** One of the diagonals of $Q$ is a line of symmetry of $Q$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II.** The midpoints of the sides of $Q$ are the vertices of a square.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Decide whether each is necessarily true, with a single counterexample if possible.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** What shape **are** the midpoints always the vertices of, given perpendicular diagonals?
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** What extra hypothesis makes II true?

[Adapted from **2018 P2 Q5**, which poses exactly statements I and II; the shape of the midpoint quadrilateral and the repair are added.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** Put the diagonals along the axes — which is exactly what "perpendicular" allows:

$$P(-1,0),\quad Q(0,2),\quad R(3,0),\quad S(0,-5).$$

The diagonals $PR$ and $QS$ lie along the axes, so they are perpendicular ✓.

**I is false.** Reflecting in $PR$ (the $x$-axis) sends $Q(0,2)$ to $(0,-2)$, which is not $S(0,-5)$.
Reflecting in $QS$ (the $y$-axis) sends $P(-1,0)$ to $(1,0)$, which is not $R(3,0)$. *Neither diagonal is an
axis — a kite has one, but perpendicular diagonals alone do not make a kite.*

**II is false.** The four midpoints are $\left(-\tfrac12,1\right)$, $\left(\tfrac32,1\right)$,
$\left(\tfrac32,-\tfrac52\right)$, $\left(-\tfrac12,-\tfrac52\right)$ — a rectangle with sides $2$ and
$\tfrac72$, not a square.

$$\boxed{\text{neither I nor II}}$$

**(b)** For **any** quadrilateral the midpoints form a parallelogram whose sides are parallel to the
diagonals (Varignon). If the diagonals are perpendicular, those sides are perpendicular too:

$$\boxed{\text{always a rectangle}}$$

**(c)** The midpoint rectangle's side lengths are **half the diagonals**, so it is a square exactly when

$$\boxed{\text{the diagonals are also equal in length}}$$

*In the counterexample $\lvert PR\rvert=4$ and $\lvert QS\rvert=7$ — perpendicular but unequal, which is why
II failed.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The diagonal table — these are the *iff*s ★

| diagonals | shape guaranteed |
|---|---|
| bisect each other | parallelogram |
| bisect **and equal** | rectangle |
| bisect **and perpendicular** | rhombus |
| bisect, equal **and** perpendicular | square |
| one perpendicularly bisects the other | kite |

Read each as **at least** that shape — a square satisfies every row. Most nec/suff options on the paper are
one of these rows, altered.

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
$PQRS$ is a **parallelogram**, labelled anticlockwise. Consider

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I.** $\lvert PQ\rvert=\lvert QR\rvert$ &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
**II.** $PR$ meets $QS$ at right angles &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
**III.** $\angle PQR=\angle QRS$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Which conditions, taken **individually**, are sufficient for $PQRS$ to be a square?
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** For each, name the shape it does force.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Which **pairs** are sufficient for a square?

[Adapted from **2020 P2 Q7**, which asks only about the three conditions individually.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** $\boxed{\text{none of them}}$

**(b)**

| | forces | why it is not enough |
|---|---|---|
| I | **rhombus** | adjacent sides equal, but the angles are unconstrained |
| II | **rhombus** | perpendicular diagonals characterise a rhombus among parallelograms |
| III | **rectangle** | see below |

For III: consecutive angles of a parallelogram are **supplementary**, so
$\angle PQR+\angle QRS=180^{\circ}$. Combined with equality,

$$2\angle PQR=180^{\circ}\ \Longrightarrow\ \angle PQR=90^{\circ},$$

a rectangle — and a $4\times2$ rectangle is not a square.

*A rhombus that is not a square:* $P(0,0),Q(5,0),R(8,4),S(3,4)$ — all four sides $5$, diagonals
perpendicular, angles not right.

**(c)** A square is precisely **rhombus and rectangle**, so a pair works exactly when it supplies both:

$$\boxed{\text{I}+\text{III}\ \text{ and }\ \text{II}+\text{III}}$$

*I$+$II fails: both only give a rhombus, so together they still give a rhombus. Two conditions that force
the same thing are worth no more than one.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Forcing a parallelogram

**Sufficient, each alone:** both pairs of sides parallel · both pairs equal · the **same one pair** both
equal **and** parallel · diagonals bisect each other.

**Not sufficient — the exam's favourite:** one pair *equal* and a **different** pair *parallel*
($AB=CD$ but $AD\parallel BC$). That describes an **isosceles trapezium**.

*Splitting "equal" and "parallel" across different pairs is the whole trap.*

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
Let $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ have position vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Prove that $ABCD$ (in that order) is a parallelogram if and only if
$\vec a+\vec c=\vec b+\vec d$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Decide whether $A(1,2)$, $B(4,3)$, $C(6,7)$, $D(3,6)$ is a parallelogram.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Prove that the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other **if and only if** it is a
parallelogram.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** Explain why the test in (a) would wrongly accept the points if they were given in the
order $A$, $B$, $D$, $C$.

[Adapted from **2019 P2 Q10** and **2020 P2 Q7**, both of which hinge on the anticlockwise labelling.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** $ABCD$ is a parallelogram exactly when $\vec{AB}=\vec{DC}$, that is

$$\vec b-\vec a=\vec c-\vec d\ \iff\ \boxed{\vec a+\vec c=\vec b+\vec d}$$

*Both sides equal twice the midpoint of a diagonal, which is the content of (c).*

**(b)** $\vec a+\vec c=(1,2)+(6,7)=(7,9)$ and $\vec b+\vec d=(4,3)+(3,6)=(7,9)$:

$$\boxed{\text{yes, a parallelogram}}$$

**(c)** The midpoint of $AC$ is $\tfrac12(\vec a+\vec c)$ and the midpoint of $BD$ is
$\tfrac12(\vec b+\vec d)$. These coincide exactly when $\vec a+\vec c=\vec b+\vec d$, which by (a) is exactly
the parallelogram condition. $\blacksquare$

*Note this is a genuine **iff**, proved in one line in both directions — unlike the near-misses in the
lattice card.*

**(d)** The condition $\vec a+\vec c=\vec b+\vec d$ pairs $A$ with $C$ and $B$ with $D$ — it tests whether
**those** are the diagonals.

$$\boxed{\text{Relabelling changes which pairs count as diagonals.}}$$

With the order $A,B,D,C$ the diagonals are $AD$ and $BC$, so the correct test becomes
$\vec a+\vec d=\vec b+\vec c$: here $(4,8)\ne(10,10)$, and indeed $ABDC$ is a self-crossing quadrilateral.
*The vertex order is part of the hypothesis, which is why every exam question specifies "labelled
anticlockwise".*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Congruence, and the one that is not ★

**Criteria:** SSS · SAS · ASA · AAS · RHS.

**SSA is not a criterion** — two sides and a *non-included* angle give the ambiguous case, two triangles.

**Equal area is not a criterion either:** $\tfrac12ab\sin C$ equal gives only $\sin C_1=\sin C_2$, and

$$\sin A=\sin B\iff B=A\ \text{ or }\ B=180^\circ-A .$$

*Whenever an angle is recovered from a sine, stop — there are two possibilities.*

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
In triangle $PQR$, $PR=2$, $QR=p$ and $\angle RPQ=30^{\circ}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Show that $PQ$ satisfies $PQ^{2}-2\sqrt3\,PQ+\left(4-p^{2}\right)=0$, and solve for
$PQ$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Hence find the complete set of $p$ for which the given information determines the
triangle **uniquely**.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** For which $p$ is there no triangle at all, and for which are there exactly two?
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** Which congruence criterion is being tested, and why is it not a criterion?

[Adapted from **2018 P2 Q14**, which asks only for the set of $p$ giving a unique triangle.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** Cosine rule at $P$, with $\cos30^{\circ}=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$:

$$p^{2}=2^{2}+PQ^{2}-2(2)(PQ)\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\ \Longrightarrow\ PQ^{2}-2\sqrt3\,PQ+\left(4-p^{2}\right)=0 .$$

$$PQ=\sqrt3\pm\sqrt{3-\left(4-p^{2}\right)}=\boxed{\sqrt3\pm\sqrt{p^{2}-1}}$$

**(b)** We need exactly one **positive** root.

| $p$ | $\sqrt{p^{2}-1}$ | roots $\sqrt3\pm\sqrt{p^{2}-1}$ | triangles |
|---|---|---|---|
| $p<1$ | not real | — | $0$ |
| $p=1$ | $0$ | $\sqrt3$ (repeated) | $1$ |
| $1<p<2$ | $0<\cdot<\sqrt3$ | both positive | $2$ |
| $p=2$ | $\sqrt3$ | $2\sqrt3$ and $0$ | $1$ |
| $p>2$ | $>\sqrt3$ | one positive, one negative | $1$ |

$$\boxed{p=1\ \text{ or }\ p\ge2}$$

**(c)** $\boxed{\text{no triangle for }p<1;\quad\text{exactly two for }1<p<2}$

*The value $p=1$ is the perpendicular distance from $R$ to the line $PQ$, namely $PR\sin30^{\circ}=1$ — below
it the side cannot reach, at it the triangle is right-angled, just above it there are two positions.*

**(d)** The data is two sides and a **non-included** angle, $\boxed{\text{SSA}}$ — the one arrangement that
is not a congruence criterion. *SAS, ASA, SSS and RHS all determine a triangle; SSA leaves the ambiguous
case above, and the algebra shows it as a quadratic with two positive roots.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The midpoint quadrilateral ★

Join the midpoints of the sides of **any** quadrilateral: the result is **always a parallelogram**, with its
sides parallel to the diagonals and half their length.

| condition on the diagonals of $ABCD$ | midpoint quadrilateral |
|---|---|
| none | parallelogram |
| equal | **rhombus** |
| perpendicular | **rectangle** |
| equal **and** perpendicular | **square** |

*Each row is an **iff**, so this converts a fact about the diagonals into one about the sides and back.*

[equal gives the rhombus, perpendicular gives the rectangle — not the other way round]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Prove that the midpoints of the sides of **any** quadrilateral are the vertices of a
parallelogram, and say what its sides are parallel to.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** State the condition on the original quadrilateral for the midpoint parallelogram to be
(i) a rectangle, (ii) a rhombus, (iii) a square.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Prove that the midpoint parallelogram always has **half** the area of the original.

[Adapted from **2018 P2 Q5**, whose statement II is the square case of part (b).]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** Let the vertices be $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$ and the midpoints
$\vec m_1=\tfrac12(\vec a+\vec b)$, $\vec m_2=\tfrac12(\vec b+\vec c)$, $\vec m_3=\tfrac12(\vec c+\vec d)$,
$\vec m_4=\tfrac12(\vec d+\vec a)$. Then

$$\vec m_2-\vec m_1=\tfrac12(\vec c-\vec a)=\vec m_3-\vec m_4 .$$

*One pair of opposite sides equal **and** parallel,* so it is a parallelogram. Moreover each side is
parallel to a **diagonal** of the original, and half its length:

$$\boxed{\text{sides parallel to }AC\text{ and }BD,\text{ of half their lengths}}$$

**(b)** Since the sides carry the directions and half the lengths of the diagonals:

| midpoint shape | condition on the original |
|---|---|
| (i) rectangle | the diagonals are **perpendicular** |
| (ii) rhombus | the diagonals are **equal in length** |
| (iii) square | the diagonals are **perpendicular and equal** |

*Note the swap — perpendicular diagonals give equal **angles** in the midpoint figure, equal diagonals give
equal **sides**.*

**(c)** The parallelogram has sides $\tfrac12\vec{AC}$ and $\tfrac12\vec{BD}$, so its area is

$$\left\lvert\tfrac12\vec{AC}\times\tfrac12\vec{BD}\right\rvert=\tfrac14\left\lvert\vec{AC}\times\vec{BD}\right\rvert .$$

For any quadrilateral the area is $\tfrac12\left\lvert\vec{AC}\times\vec{BD}\right\rvert$. Hence

$$\boxed{\text{midpoint area}=\tfrac12\times\text{original area}}$$

*Independent of the shape — which makes it a useful check in any question that builds a figure from
midpoints.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Polygons and circles

$$\text{interior sum}=(n-2)\times180^\circ\qquad\text{regular interior}=180^\circ-\frac{360^\circ}{n}$$

$n=3,4,5,6,8,12\Rightarrow60^\circ,90^\circ,108^\circ,120^\circ,135^\circ,150^\circ$.

**Pentagon consequence:** five angles in arithmetic progression sum to $5a=540^\circ$, so the **middle one
is forced to be $108^\circ$**, whatever the common difference.

**Equal areas from the centre $\neq$ regular:** each central angle is $\alpha$ or $180^\circ-\alpha$, so
only $n=3$ forces regularity. For $n=4$, angles $60,120,60,120$ work.

**Cyclic quadrilateral:** opposite angles sum to $180^\circ$ — a genuine *iff*.

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Consider this statement about a pentagon $P$:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$(\ast)$ if at least one interior angle of $P$ is $108^{\circ}$, then **all** its
interior angles are $108^{\circ}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;Decide $(\ast)$, giving a counterexample if it is false, and write its contrapositive.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** A convex polygon has all its vertices on a circle and all its sides equal. Prove it is
regular.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Is "all interior angles equal" sufficient for a cyclic polygon to be regular?

[Adapted from **2023 P2 Q9** (the pentagon statement) and **2022 P2 Q19** (a polygon with every vertex on a circle).]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** **False.** The interior angles of a pentagon sum to $540^{\circ}$, and

$$\boxed{108^{\circ},\ 100^{\circ},\ 110^{\circ},\ 112^{\circ},\ 110^{\circ}}$$

sums to $540^{\circ}$ with one angle equal to $108^{\circ}$ and the rest not. *The angle sum is the only
constraint, and it leaves enormous freedom — fixing one angle fixes nothing else.*

Contrapositive: *if not all the interior angles of $P$ are $108^{\circ}$, then none of them is
$108^{\circ}$.* (Equally false, as it must be.)

**(b)** Equal chords of a circle subtend equal arcs, so all $n$ arcs between consecutive vertices are
equal. An inscribed angle depends only on the arc it stands on, and each interior angle stands on the arc
made of the other $n-2$ pieces — the same in every case. So all the interior angles are equal as well, and
the polygon is $\boxed{\text{regular}}$. $\blacksquare$

**(c)** **No.** $$\boxed{\text{A }4\times2\text{ rectangle}}$$

is cyclic with every angle $90^{\circ}$, yet it is not regular. *Equal sides plus cyclic gives regular;
equal angles plus cyclic does not. The two halves of "regular" are not interchangeable — and for a
**triangle** either one suffices, which is where the false intuition comes from.*
:::

# Part 4 · The recurring mathematical engines

*Paper 2 recombines a short reasoning list with ordinary Paper 1 mathematics. The cards below are not a
second Paper 1 formula sheet: they are the moves that repeatedly decide the reasoning questions.*

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · Applications and reasoning</div>
<div class="fs-title">Eight engines that carry the logic</div>
<div class="fs-sub">For each one: remember the fact, recognise the question shape, then use the routine.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Roots and graphs ★

**Formula / facts**

$$f(x)=0\iff\text{$x$-intercept},\qquad f'(x)=0\iff\text{stationary point}.$$

A degree-$n$ polynomial has at most $n$ real roots. Between two distinct roots of differentiable $f$ lies
a root of $f'$ (Rolle), so $n$ distinct roots of $f$ force at least $n-1$ roots of $f'$.

**Never reverse it:** a stationary point need not give two roots. $f(x)=x^2+1$ has $f'(0)=0$ but no real
root.

**Frequent type — “how many roots are possible?”** Sketch the simplest allowed shape; count intersections,
not algebraic solutions. Use end behaviour + turning points + tangencies. A repeated root touches; a simple
root crosses.

[example: $x|x|=px+q$ means intersect the two-branch graph $y=x|x|$ with a line]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
Let $f$ be a non-constant polynomial and $g(x)=x\,f'(x)$. Suppose $f(x)=0$ for exactly $M$ real values of
$x$, and $g(x)=0$ for exactly $N$ real values of $x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Decide which of $M<N$, $M=N$, $M>N$ are possible, giving an explicit $f$ for each.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Prove that $N\ge M-1$ always.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Show that $N-M$ can be made as large as we please.

[Adapted from **2023 P2 Q19**, which asks only which of the three comparisons are possible.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** *All three are possible — and three quadratics settle it.* In every case $g(x)=2x^{2}$, whose only
real zero is $x=0$, so $N=1$.

| $f$ | real roots of $f$ | $M$ | $N$ | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $x^{2}+1$ | none | $0$ | $1$ | $M<N$ |
| $x^{2}$ | $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $M=N$ |
| $x^{2}-1$ | $\pm1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $M>N$ |

$$\boxed{\text{all three}}$$

*Note that $M$ counts **distinct** roots, so the repeated root of $x^{2}$ contributes $1$, not $2$.*

**(b)** The zeros of $g$ are $x=0$ together with the zeros of $f'$. If $f$ has $M$ distinct real roots, then
between each consecutive pair Rolle's theorem supplies a zero of $f'$ — at least $M-1$ of them, all distinct.
Hence

$$N\ \ge\ \#\{\text{zeros of }f'\}\ \ge\ M-1 .$$

$$\boxed{N\ge M-1}$$

*The deficit of exactly $1$ is achieved when $0$ happens to be one of those zeros of $f'$, as in the third
row above.*

**(c)** Take $f$ with **no** real roots but many turning points, so $M=0$ while $N$ is large. For instance

$$f(x)=\left(x^{2}+1\right)\left(x^{2}+4\right)\cdots\left(x^{2}+k^{2}\right)$$

has $M=0$, while $f'$ is an odd polynomial of degree $2k-1$ and may have up to $2k-1$ real zeros.

$$\boxed{N-M\text{ is unbounded}}$$

*So the inequality in (b) is one-sided: $N$ can fall below $M$ by at most $1$, but exceed it without
limit.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Calculus conditions ★

**Formula / facts**

$$f'(a)=0\text{ is necessary, not sufficient, for an interior differentiable maximum/minimum.}$$
$$f''(a)>0\Rightarrow\text{local minimum},\qquad f''(a)<0\Rightarrow\text{local maximum}.$$

$f''(a)=0$ alone proves nothing: $x^4$ has a minimum at $0$; $x^3$ has an inflection there.
An inflection needs **concavity to change sign**. Increasing means $f'\ge0$ (strictly increasing does not
require $f'>0$ at every point: $x^3$ is the standard counterexample).

**Frequent type — necessary or sufficient?** Translate the geometric word into its exact derivative
condition, then test both arrows with $x^2$, $x^3$, $x^4$ or a constant function.

[memory: stationary = flat; turning = changes direction; inflection = changes bend]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
Let $f$ be a polynomial and consider

$$P:\ f(x)=0\text{ for exactly three real values of }x,\qquad
Q:\ f'(x)=0\text{ for exactly two real values of }x .$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Is $P$ sufficient for $Q$? Justify with a polynomial if not.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Is $P$ necessary for $Q$? Justify with a polynomial if not.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** State the correct relationship, and say what extra hypothesis would make $P$ and $Q$
equivalent.

[Adapted from **2021 P2 Q6**, which asks for the classification only; the two witnesses are supplied here.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** **Not sufficient.** Take

$$\boxed{f(x)=x(x-1)^{2}(x+1)^{2}}$$

Its distinct real roots are $-1,0,1$, so $P$ holds. But $f$ has degree $5$ and $f'$ has **four** distinct
real zeros — the two repeated roots are themselves stationary points, and Rolle adds one in each of the two
gaps. So $Q$ fails.

*Repeated roots are the loophole: they are roots **and** turning points at once.*

**(b)** **Not necessary.** Take

$$\boxed{f(x)=x^{3}-3x+10}$$

Here $f'(x)=3x^{2}-3$ has exactly two zeros, $x=\pm1$, so $Q$ holds. But the local maximum
$f(-1)=12$ and the local minimum $f(1)=8$ are **both positive**, so the curve crosses the axis once only:
$f$ has exactly **one** real root and $P$ fails.

**(c)** $$\boxed{P\text{ is neither necessary nor sufficient for }Q}$$

For a **cubic**, however, three distinct real roots and two stationary points are equivalent: a cubic with
three distinct roots must have two turning points (Rolle), and a cubic with two turning points has three
distinct roots exactly when the two stationary values have opposite signs.

$$\boxed{\text{restrict to cubics }\textbf{and}\text{ require stationary values of opposite signs}}$$

*The general-polynomial version fails in both directions, and for opposite reasons — multiplicity in (a),
the position of the turning values in (b).*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Inequalities and domains ★

**Safe moves:** add the same expression; multiply by a known positive number; square only after controlling
signs. Multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the sign.

$$a^2\ge0,\qquad (a-b)^2\ge0\Rightarrow a^2+b^2\ge2ab,$$
$$\sqrt{X}=|Y|\text{ when }X=Y^2,\qquad \cos x=\pm\sqrt{1-\sin^2x}.$$

**Domains:** denominators $\ne0$; square-root inputs $\ge0$; logarithm inputs $>0$. For $0<a<1$,
$\log_a x$ is decreasing, so an inequality reverses when applying it.

**Frequent type — first error.** Annotate every risky line with its missing condition: “divisor non-zero?”,
“both sides non-negative?”, “log base above 1?”, “domain retained?”. Stop at the first missing condition.

[counterexample to multiplying inequalities: $-3<-2$ and $-1<0$, but $3\not<0$]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Solve $\lvert x+5\rvert<\lvert x+11\rvert$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Solve $\lvert x+11\rvert<\lvert x+1\rvert$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Hence describe the set of real numbers satisfying **both**, and state its length.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** Explain why squaring both sides is legitimate here but not in
$\lvert x+5\rvert<x+11$.

[Adapted from **2022 P2 Q14**, which gives exactly these two inequalities and asks for the length of the overlap.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

*For a modulus inequality between two moduli, square — both sides are non-negative, so squaring is
reversible.*

**(a)** $(x+5)^{2}<(x+11)^{2}$ gives $10x+25<22x+121$, i.e. $-96<12x$:

$$\boxed{x>-8}$$

*Geometrically: $x$ is closer to $-5$ than to $-11$, so it lies on the $-5$ side of the midpoint $-8$.*

**(b)** $(x+11)^{2}<(x+1)^{2}$ gives $22x+121<2x+1$, i.e. $20x<-120$:

$$\boxed{x<-6}$$

**(c)** $$\boxed{-8<x<-6,\ \text{ an interval of length }2}$$

**(d)** Squaring $\lvert A\rvert<\lvert B\rvert$ is an **equivalence**, because $t\mapsto t^{2}$ is strictly
increasing on $[0,\infty)$ and both sides are already non-negative.

In $\lvert x+5\rvert<x+11$ the right-hand side is **not** known to be non-negative.

$$\boxed{\text{Squaring is only valid once }x+11\ge0\text{ has been imposed.}}$$

*With $x<-11$ the inequality is false outright, since a modulus cannot be less than a negative number —
and squaring would silently lose that case. Correctly: $x\ge-11$ and $(x+5)^{2}<(x+11)^{2}$, giving
$x>-8$.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Transformations and solution counts

Horizontal shifts, reflections and non-zero stretches preserve the **number** of roots:

$$f(x-a)=0,\quad f(-x)=0,\quad f(kx)=0\ (k\ne0)$$

are re-labellings of the roots of $f$. A vertical shift $f(x)+c=0$ can change the count.

Inverse graphs reflect in $y=x$, so $f(x)=x$ and $f^{-1}(x)=x$ have the same fixed points (when the inverse
exists). But squaring or modulus can add a branch:

$$|f(x)|=k\iff f(x)=\pm k\qquad(k\ge0).$$

**Frequent type — “same number of solutions”.** Substitute to expose a bijection between solution sets.
If the manipulation introduces $\pm$, squares, or discards a domain, count the new branches separately.

[example: $\cos^2x=c^2$ means $\cos x=c$ or $\cos x=-c$]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
Let $p$ and $q$ be real and suppose $x\lvert x\rvert=px+q$ has exactly $k$ distinct real solutions.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Explain why $y=x\lvert x\rvert$ is strictly increasing, and describe its shape either
side of the origin.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Find the largest possible value of $k$, giving $p$ and $q$ that achieve it.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Prove that $k=4$ is impossible.

[Adapted from **2021 P2 Q16**, which asks for the largest possible number of solutions of this equation.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** $$x\lvert x\rvert=\begin{cases}x^{2}&x\ge0\\[2pt]-x^{2}&x<0\end{cases}$$

Both branches increase, and they agree at $0$, so the function is strictly increasing throughout. It is
**convex** on $x\ge0$ (the right half of $y=x^{2}$) and **concave** on $x\le0$:

$$\boxed{\text{an odd, strictly increasing curve with an inflection at the origin}}$$

**(b)** Split the equation at $0$:

$$x\ge0:\ x^{2}-px-q=0,\qquad x<0:\ x^{2}+px+q=0 .$$

Take $p=3$, $q=-2$. The first becomes $x^{2}-3x+2=0$, with roots $1$ and $2$, both $\ge0$ ✓. The second
becomes $x^{2}+3x-2=0$, with roots $\tfrac{-3\pm\sqrt{17}}{2}$, of which only
$\tfrac{-3-\sqrt{17}}{2}\approx-3.56$ is negative ✓.

$$\boxed{k=3,\text{ achieved at }p=3,\ q=-2}$$

**(c)** $k=4$ would need **two** roots $\ge0$ from $x^{2}-px-q=0$ and **two** roots $<0$ from
$x^{2}+px+q=0$. Comparing the products of the roots:

$$\text{two non-negative roots}\Rightarrow -q\ge0,\qquad
\text{two negative roots}\Rightarrow q>0 .$$

$$\boxed{q\le0\text{ and }q>0\text{ cannot both hold, so }k\le3 .}$$

*A line can cut a convex arc twice and a concave arc twice, so $4$ looks available — the sign of $q$ is what
forbids it.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}

### Trigonometric counting ★

$$\sin u=\sin\alpha\Rightarrow u=\alpha+360^\circ k\text{ or }180^\circ-\alpha+360^\circ k,$$
$$\cos u=\cos\alpha\Rightarrow u=\pm\alpha+360^\circ k.$$

For $u=mx+c$, **transform the interval first**, solve in $u$, then convert back. Endpoints matter.

**Frequent type — number of solutions / sufficient condition.** Draw one-period graphs and count horizontal
line intersections. Split squares or modulus into $+$ and $-$ levels before counting.

**Two traps:** $\sin A=\sin B$ does not force $A=B$; and $\sqrt{\cos^2x}=|\cos x|$, not $\cos x$.

[memory: equation in $2x$ over $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$ spans two full turns]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
The angle $\theta$ takes each of the values $1^{\circ},2^{\circ},\dots,360^{\circ}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Simplify
$\ \sin\theta\sqrt{1+\sin\theta}\,\sqrt{1-\sin\theta}+\cos\theta\sqrt{1+\cos\theta}\,\sqrt{1-\cos\theta}$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** For how many of the $360$ values is the expression zero?
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Why is the answer not $180$?

[Adapted from **2021 P2 Q19**, which gives the same expression and asks for the count.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** $\sqrt{1+s}\,\sqrt{1-s}=\sqrt{1-s^{2}}$, and *the square root is the non-negative one*, so

$$\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}\theta}=\lvert\cos\theta\rvert,\qquad\sqrt{1-\cos^{2}\theta}=\lvert\sin\theta\rvert .$$

$$\boxed{\sin\theta\lvert\cos\theta\rvert+\cos\theta\lvert\sin\theta\rvert}$$

**(b)** Work quadrant by quadrant, since only the **signs** matter.

| quadrant | $\sin$ | $\cos$ | expression | zero? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $+$ | $+$ | $2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ | no |
| 2 | $+$ | $-$ | $-\sin\theta\cos\theta+\cos\theta\sin\theta=0$ | **yes, always** |
| 3 | $-$ | $-$ | $-2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ | no |
| 4 | $-$ | $+$ | $\sin\theta\cos\theta-\cos\theta\sin\theta=0$ | **yes, always** |

Counting the integer degrees: quadrant 2 contributes $91^{\circ}$ to $179^{\circ}$, which is $89$ values,
and quadrant 4 contributes $271^{\circ}$ to $359^{\circ}$, another $89$. The four axis values
$90^{\circ},180^{\circ},270^{\circ},360^{\circ}$ all give $0$ as well, since one of $\sin\theta$,
$\cos\theta$ vanishes.

$$\boxed{89+89+4=182}$$

**(c)** Two separate reasons pull away from a naive "half of $360$":

$$\boxed{\text{the open quadrants hold }89\text{ integers, not }90\text{ — and the four axis values also work.}}$$

*The expression vanishes exactly when $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ have **opposite** signs or one of them is
zero. Listing the boundary cases separately is the whole question.*
:::

### Sequences, invariants and pigeonholes

For a recurrence, calculate only enough terms to guess what cannot change: parity, remainder, sign, gcd, or
a bounded range. Then prove that property survives one recurrence step.

$$\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(b,a+kb),\qquad \text{consecutive recurrence terms often carry the same gcd.}$$

**Pigeonhole principle:** putting $N$ objects into $k$ boxes forces some box to contain at least
$\lceil N/k\rceil$ objects. For “must occur”, choose boxes so one overfull box is exactly the desired pair.

**Frequent type — which must be true?** Search for an invariant before testing long lists. For a claimed
possibility, build one short example; for a necessity, try extremes and equality cases first.

[example: residues mod $m$ are the $m$ boxes; $m+1$ integers force two equal residues]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
A large circular table has $40$ chairs around it.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Translate "the next person to sit down **must** sit next to someone" into a condition on
the gaps between the people already seated.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Find the smallest number of people for which this is possible.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Answer the same question for $40$ chairs in a **row**, and explain why the two answers
agree even though the gap structure differs.

[Adapted from **2019 P2 Q9**, which asks only for the circular case.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** A newcomer can avoid everyone exactly when some empty chair has **both** neighbours empty — that is,
when three consecutive chairs are free. So the requirement is

$$\boxed{\text{every gap between consecutive occupied chairs contains at most }2\text{ empty chairs.}}$$

**(b)** With $n$ people around the circle there are exactly $n$ gaps, holding $40-n$ empty chairs in total.
Each gap holds at most $2$, so

$$40-n\le2n\ \Longrightarrow\ n\ge\frac{40}{3}=13.\dot3 .$$

$$\boxed{n=14}$$

*And $14$ is attainable:* $26$ empty chairs over $14$ gaps, for instance twelve gaps of $2$ and two of $1$.
With $13$ people the gaps could hold at most $26$ chairs but $27$ are empty, so some gap reaches $3$. ✓

**(c)** In a row there are $n+1$ gaps, but the two **end** gaps may hold only $1$ chair each — the chair at
the very end of the row has a single neighbour, so two free chairs there are already enough to hide in.
Hence

$$40-n\le\underbrace{1+1}_{\text{ends}}+\underbrace{2(n-1)}_{\text{interior}}=2n ,$$

$$\boxed{n=14\text{ again}}$$

*The two $1$s lost at the ends are exactly balanced by having one gap fewer in the interior — the bound
$40-n\le2n$ comes out identical. (Checked by exhaustive search for $9$, $12$ and $15$ chairs, where circle
and row both give $\lceil N/3\rceil$.)*
:::

### Integrals without full calculation

$$\int_a^b(f(x)+c)\,dx=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx+c(b-a),$$
$$\int_{-a}^{a}\!f(x)\,dx=0\text{ if $f$ is odd},\qquad
\int_{-a}^{a}\!f(x)\,dx=2\int_0^a\!f(x)\,dx\text{ if $f$ is even}.$$

If $f\le g$ throughout $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b f\le\int_a^b g$. An integral is **signed area**: below
the axis contributes negatively.

**Frequent type — compare / infer without integrating.** Simplify the integrand first; look for symmetry,
a constant vertical shift, or a pointwise inequality. For $f(|x|)$, mirror the right half; split at $0$.

[example: replacing $f$ by $f+C$ adds the rectangle $C(b-a)$]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Place these in increasing order **without evaluating any of them**, justifying each
comparison:

$$P=\int_0^1 2^{x^{2}}\,\mathrm dx,\qquad Q=\int_0^1 2^{x}\,\mathrm dx,\qquad R=\int_0^1\left(2^{x}\right)^{2}\mathrm dx .$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Evaluate $Q$ and $R$ exactly, and confirm the order.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Show that $\displaystyle\int_0^1\sin x\,\mathrm dx<\tfrac12$ without evaluating the
integral.

[Adapted from **2022 P2 Q12**, which asks for three such integrals to be placed in order of size, and **2023 P2 Q20**.]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** *Compare the integrands pointwise on the open interval; the integrals then inherit the order.*

For $0<x<1$ we have $x^{2}<x<2x$, and $t\mapsto2^{t}$ is strictly increasing, so

$$2^{x^{2}}<2^{x}<2^{2x}=\left(2^{x}\right)^{2}.$$

Integrating over $[0,1]$ preserves strict inequality between continuous functions that differ somewhere:

$$\boxed{P<Q<R}$$

**(b)** $$Q=\left[\frac{2^{x}}{\ln2}\right]_0^1=\frac{1}{\ln2}\approx1.4427,$$
$$R=\int_0^1 4^{x}\,\mathrm dx=\left[\frac{4^{x}}{\ln4}\right]_0^1=\frac{3}{2\ln2}\approx2.1640 .$$

Numerically $P\approx1.2882$, so $1.2882<1.4427<2.1640$ ✓. *$P$ has no elementary antiderivative at all —
which is exactly why the question asks for an ordering rather than a value.*

**(c)** For $0<x\le1$, $\sin x<x$. *(The functions agree at $0$ and $\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\sin x=\cos
x<1$ thereafter.)* Hence

$$\int_0^1\sin x\,\mathrm dx<\int_0^1 x\,\mathrm dx=\boxed{\tfrac12}$$

*Check:* the true value is $1-\cos1\approx0.4597$ ✓.
:::

### Lines and circles as conditions

For $ax+by=c$ ($a,b\ne0$):

$$m=-\frac ab,\qquad x\text{-intercept}=\frac ca,\qquad y\text{-intercept}=\frac cb.$$

Perpendicular lines satisfy $m_1m_2=-1$. A circle tangent to an axis has
**distance from centre to the axis = radius**.

**Frequent type — necessary/sufficient data.** Convert each geometric statement to one algebraic equation,
then ask whether it determines the target uniquely. If free variables remain, it is not sufficient.

**Cyclic invariant:** for gradients $-a/b,-b/c,-c/a$, the product is $-1$ — simplify the whole cycle
before testing cases.

[sign trap: positive gradient tells the signs of $a,b$ are opposite, but not the sign of $c$]{.eg}

#### Challenge &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">harder</span>
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** A circle has equation $(x-9)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}=4$, and a square has vertices $(1,0)$,
$(1,2)$, $(-1,2)$, $(-1,0)$. A straight line bisects the area of **both**. Explain why the line is uniquely
determined, and find where it crosses the $x$-axis.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** The circle $x^{2}+ax+y^{2}+by+c=0$ has non-zero real constants $a,b,c$. Find a
necessary and sufficient condition for it to be **tangent to the $y$-axis**.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** State the corresponding condition for tangency to the $x$-axis, and the condition for
the circle to touch **both** axes.

[Adapted from **2021 P2 Q7** (the bisecting line) and **2021 P2 Q15** (the tangency condition).]{.eg}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** *A line bisects the area of a centrally symmetric region if and only if it passes through the
centre* — reflecting in the centre swaps the two parts. The circle's centre is $(9,-2)$ and the square's is
$(0,1)$, so the line must pass through both. Two distinct points determine one line, hence uniqueness.

$$\text{gradient}=\frac{1-(-2)}{0-9}=-\frac13,\qquad y=-\frac{x}{3}+1 .$$

Setting $y=0$:

$$\boxed{x=3}$$

**(b)** Completing the square, the centre is $\left(-\tfrac a2,-\tfrac b2\right)$ and

$$r^{2}=\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{4}-c .$$

Tangency to the $y$-axis means the distance from the centre to $x=0$ equals the radius, i.e.
$\left\lvert\tfrac a2\right\rvert=r$:

$$\frac{a^{2}}{4}=\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{4}-c\ \Longrightarrow\ \boxed{b^{2}=4c}$$

*The $a^{2}$ cancels, which is the surprise — the condition involves only $b$ and $c$. Note $c>0$ follows,
and $r=\left\lvert\tfrac a2\right\rvert>0$ since $a\ne0$, so it is a genuine circle.*

**(c)** By symmetry, swapping the roles of $a$ and $b$:

$$\boxed{\text{tangent to the }x\text{-axis}\iff a^{2}=4c}$$

Touching both axes requires both, so $a^{2}=b^{2}=4c$, i.e.

$$\boxed{a=\pm b\ \text{ with }\ c=\frac{a^{2}}{4}}$$

*Then the centre is equidistant from the two axes and the circle sits in one quadrant, inscribed in the
corner.*
:::

# Part 5 · The exam-day card

::: {.callout-important}
## Before you read a single question

Write these at the top of your rough paper:

1. $\;$ **sufficient $\to$ forwards, necessary $\to$ backwards**
2. $\;$ **contrapositive = equivalent; converse = trap**
3. $\;$ $\lnot(P\Rightarrow Q)=P$ **and** $\lnot Q$
4. $\;$ **rhombus · rectangle · isosceles trapezium** — the three counterexamples
5. $\;$ $p$ divides $ab$ $\Rightarrow$ $p$ divides $a$ or $p$ divides $b$ — **only for prime $p$**
6. $\;$ $\sqrt{u^2}=|u|$ · $f'(a)=0$ is not automatically a turn · check every domain
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## The thirty-second routine for any Paper 2 question

**Name the reasoning type first, then do the mathematics.** Almost every lost mark comes from competent
mathematics done on the wrong question.

| The question says… | It is asking for… | So you… |
|---|---|---|
| "necessary", "sufficient" | set inclusion | find the **exact** set, then compare |
| "must be true" | $\forall$ | find a counterexample, or prove it |
| "possible", "can" | $\exists$ | **produce one witness** |
| "which is equivalent" | contrapositive | negate both halves and reverse |
| "first error", "best describes" | Err1/Err2 | read down, stop at the first failure |
| "number of solutions" | intersections | sketch, transform the interval, count branches |
| "same number of roots" | bijection | substitute; watch for $\pm$, squaring and domains |
| recurrence / long list | invariant | test parity, remainder, sign, gcd, bounds |
| no logical wording at all | Paper 1 technique | just calculate — about a quarter of the paper |
:::
